Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 26, verses 5–9:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Never does there come to them any reminder from the Most Merciful, but they turn away from it.﴾ ﴿They have indeed denied, so there will come to them the news of that at which they used to mock.﴾ ﴿Have they not looked at the earth, how many noble kinds of plants We have caused to grow in it?﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them are not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾

The first issue: His words ﴿Never does there come to them any reminder from the Most Merciful, but they turn away from it﴾ are a continuation of His words ﴿If We wish, We could send down upon them﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 4]. Thus He draws attention to the fact that, although He is able to make them believers by compulsion, He is merciful to them, in that He brings to them, state after state, the Qur'an, which is the reminder, and repeats it to them, while they remain in one and the same condition of turning away, denial and mockery. Then at that point He admonished and threatened them, because when a person persists in his disbelief, nothing benefits him except severe admonition. Therefore He said: ﴿They have indeed denied﴾, meaning: they have reached the extreme in rejecting the signs of Allah the Exalted. ﴿They have indeed denied, so there will come to them the news of that at which they used to mock.﴾ This will be either when the punishment descends upon them in this world, or at the time of direct witnessing, or in the Hereafter. It is like His words: ﴿And you will surely come to know its news after a while﴾. It is the custom regarding one who does evil to be told, as a warning: "You will see your state later." Then He, the Exalted, made clear that, along with sending down the Qur'an state after state, He has manifested proofs that occur state after state. So He said: ﴿Have they not looked at the earth, how many noble kinds of plants We have caused to grow in it?﴾ The zawj (kind, pair) is a type of plant. The karim (noble) is an attribute of everything that is pleasing and praiseworthy in its category. It is said: "a karim face" when it is pleasing in its beauty and comeliness, and "a karim book" when it is pleasing in its benefits and meanings. A karim plant is one that is pleasing in terms of the benefits connected with it. Regarding the description of the zawj as karim there are two views:

The first: plants are of two kinds, beneficial and harmful. He, glory be to Him, mentioned the abundance of what He caused to grow in the earth of all kinds of beneficial plants, and omitted mention of the harmful.

The second: He included all plants, beneficial and harmful, and described them all as noble, and drew attention to the fact that He caused nothing to grow except that it has a benefit in it, even if the heedless are unaware of it.

As for His words: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them are not believers﴾, it is like His words: ﴿a guidance for those who are mindful of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2]. The meaning is that in that there is a proof for whoever reflects and contemplates, and "most of them are not believers" means: despite all of that, most of them persist in their disbelief. As for His words: ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾, He mentioned the Mighty before the Merciful only because, had He not put it first, it might have been said that He showed mercy to them out of inability to punish them. So He removed this suspicion by mentioning the Mighty, who is the Dominant, the Irresistible; and yet He is Merciful toward His servants, for mercy that comes from complete power has a greater effect. The intended meaning is that, despite their disbelief and Allah's power to hasten their punishment, He does not withhold His mercy toward them, through what was mentioned before: the creation of every noble kind of plant, and then the bestowing of health, intellect and guidance.

The second issue: Allah the Exalted described the disbelievers first with turning away, second with denial, and third with mockery. These are the stages of one who progresses in wretchedness: he first turns away, then he openly denies and rejects, to the point that he mocks it.

The third issue: If you say, what is the meaning of combining kam (how many) with kull (every), and why did He not say: "how many noble pairs of plants We caused to grow in it"? I say: kull indicates the encompassing of the pairs of plants in detail, and kam indicates that this encompassed amount is abundant and exceedingly numerous. This is the meaning of the combination, and He arranged it upon the perfection of His power. If you say: when He mentioned the pairs and indicated them with the two words of abundance and encompassment, and they were such that none can count them except the Knower of the unseen, how then did He say: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾, and why did He not say: "signs"? I say: there are two views:

The first: that ﴿that﴾ refers to the verbal noun of "We caused to grow", so it is as if He said: indeed in that causing-to-grow is a sign, what a sign!

The second: that it is intended that in each one of those pairs there is a sign.

* * *

The fourth issue: The Mu'tazilah argued for the createdness of the Qur'an by His words: ﴿Never does there come to them any reminder from the Most Merciful, but it is newly revealed﴾. They said: the reminder is the Qur'an, by His words: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya: 50]. And in this verse He made clear that the reminder is muhdath (newly originated), so from these two verses it follows that the Qur'an is muhdath. This inference is supported by His words: ﴿Allah has sent down the best statement, a Book﴾ [al-Zumar: 23], and by His words: ﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 50]. And when it is established that it is muhdath, then it has a creator, and so it is necessarily created.

The answer: all of that refers to these words, and we grant that they are newly originated. We only claim that there is something else, eternal, beyond these letters, and there is no indication in the verse of that.

**The First Story: the story of Musa (peace be upon him)**

**Allah the Exalted said:** ﴿And when your Lord called out to Musa: "Go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Fir'awn. Will they not fear Allah?"﴾

Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah) differed over the call that Musa (peace be upon him) heard from Allah, the Exalted: is it His eternal speech (kalam qadim), or is it a kind of sound? Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari said: what was heard is the eternal speech. Just as His essence, the Exalted, is unlike all other things, even though the evidence shows that it is known and ordered, so His speech is exalted above resembling letters and sounds, even though it is heard. Abu Mansur al-Maturidi said: what Musa (peace be upon him) heard was a call of the kind of letters and sounds. This is because the evidence shows that we see substance and accident, and there must be a common cause between them for seeing to be valid, and there is no common cause except existence. So we judged that every existent can be seen. But it has not been established for us that we hear sounds and bodies, so as to rule that there must be something common between the body and the sound. Therefore it does not follow that every existent can be heard. The difference is thus clear.

As for the Mu'tazilah, they agreed that what was heard was nothing but letters and sounds. At this point they said: that call occurred in a manner by which Musa (peace be upon him) knew that it came from Allah, the Exalted, and so it was a miracle by which he knew that Allah was addressing him. He therefore did not need an intermediary. And at that time it was sufficient that He entrust him with the message, which is ﴿that you go to the wrongdoing people﴾, because at the beginning of a prophetic mission it is necessary that He command him to call to monotheism (tawhid), and after that command him with the rulings (ahkam). It is not permitted for Allah, the Exalted, to command him with this unless He had informed him that miracles would appear through him when he was challenged to produce them.

As for the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿that you go to the wrongdoing people﴾, the meaning is that He, the Exalted, branded them with wrongdoing. They deserved this description in two respects: in respect of their wronging themselves through their disbelief, and in respect of their wronging the Children of Israel.

As for His words ﴿the people of Fir'awn﴾, the phrase ﴿the people of Fir'awn﴾ is in apposition ('atf bayan) to ﴿the wrongdoing people﴾, as though "the wrongdoing people" and "the people of Fir'awn" were two expressions indicating one meaning.

* * *

As for His words ﴿Will they not fear Allah?﴾, it is read "Will they not fear Me?" (ألا يَتَّقُونِ) with a kasra on the nun, meaning ألا يَتَّقُونَنِي ("will they not fear Me"). The nun was elided because of the gathering of two nuns, and the ya' was dropped, the kasra being sufficient. His words ﴿Will they not fear Allah?﴾ are a new independent clause, which the Exalted followed with His sending him to them for warning and for branding them with wrongdoing. It expresses Musa's (peace be upon him) amazement at their condition in oppression and tyranny, and at their feeling secure from consequences and their scant fear. It is also possible that ﴿Will they not fear Allah?﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun in "the wrongdoing people", meaning: they wrong while not being mindful of Allah and His punishment. The interrogative hamza of denial (hamzat al-inkar) is then placed upon the circumstantial clause. A third view is that the meaning is: "O people, fear Me," as in His words ﴿that they should not prostrate﴾ [an-Naml 27:25].

As for the one who reads "Will you not fear Allah?" (ألا تَتَّقُونَ) in the second person, it follows the manner of iltifat (turning) towards them and turning their faces toward denial and anger against them, as one sees when a complainant complains about someone who committed a crime while the offender is present. When he gets carried away in his complaint and his anger rises, he cuts off his speech to his companion and turns to the offender, rebuking and rebuffing him, saying to him: "Will you not fear Allah? Are you not ashamed before people?" If you ask: what is the benefit of this turning and address with Musa (peace be upon him) during the time of intimate conversation, when those turned towards are absent and unaware? I answer: addressing the one sent to them in this way is, in meaning, like making it heard in their presence and conveying it to their ears, since he is their messenger and the one who relays it to them. In it there is gentleness and encouragement to increase in piety. How many a verse has been revealed concerning the disbelievers, while it contains the greatest share for the believers in reflection upon it and in drawing lessons from its contexts.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me. And my breast will be constricted, and my tongue will not be freed, so send [word] to Harun. And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me."﴾ In the verse there are several questions (masa'il).

**The first question:** Know that when God, the Exalted, commanded Musa, peace be upon him, to go to the people of Fir'awn (Pharaoh), Musa, peace be upon him, asked that Harun be sent with him to them. Then he mentioned the matters that prompted him to this request. The summary of these is that, without Harun, the purpose behind Musa's mission, peace be upon him, would have been undermined, and this is for two reasons:

The first: Fir'awn might deny him, and denial causes constriction of the heart. Constriction of the heart causes difficulty in speech for one who has an impediment in his tongue, because when the heart is constricted, the spirit and the innate heat (al-hararah al-ghariziyyah) withdraw into the inner part of the heart. When these two withdraw inward and the outer part is emptied of them, the impediment in the tongue increases. Thus, distress from denial is a cause of constriction of the heart, and constriction of the heart is a cause of the impediment. For this reason he began with fear of denial, then followed it with the constriction of the chest, then concluded with the non-freeing of the tongue. As for Harun, he is more eloquent in tongue than I am, and this meaning does not apply to him, so sending him was fitting.

The second: They have a charge against me, so I fear they will hasten to kill me, and then the purpose of the mission would not be achieved. As for Harun, this is not the case, so the purpose of the mission is attained.

**The second question:** It has been read as ﴿yadiqu﴾ and ﴿yanṭaliqu﴾ in the nominative (raf'), since they are coordinated with the predicate of inna (khabar inna). They have also been read in the accusative (nasb), coordinated with the relative clause of an-(an) (silat an). The meaning is: "I fear that they will deny me, and I fear that my breast will be constricted, and I fear that my tongue will not be freed." The difference is that the nominative reading indicates three reasons for requesting the sending of Harun, while the accusative reading indicates one reason, which is fear of these three matters. If you say: fear is distress arising from anticipating a harm that will occur, and the non-freeing of the tongue was already present, so how is fear permissible in relation to it? I reply: We have explained that the denial that will occur necessitates constriction of the heart, and constriction of the heart necessitates increased impediment. That increase was not present at the moment; rather, it was anticipated. Therefore, it is permissible to attach fear to it.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So send [word] to Harun﴾, the outward wording does not mention to whom the message is sent. In a report, God the Exalted sent Musa, peace be upon him, to him. al-Suddi said: Musa, peace be upon him, travelled with his family to Egypt and met Harun, who did not recognise him. He said, "I am Musa." They recognised each other, and he (Musa) ordered him to go with him to Fir'awn to deliver the message. Their mother cried out, fearing for them both, so they went to him. It is also possible that what is meant is: send Jibril to him, because the messenger of God to the prophets is Jibril, peace be upon him. Since he was the one specifically designated for this matter, his mention was omitted as it was known. Also, the outward wording does not state for what purpose he is to be sent; but the sense of the speech indicates that he sought assistance in what he asked, as one says when a calamity befalls you: "Send to so-and-so," meaning, "so that he may help you in it." The outward wording does not indicate that he sought Harun's being a prophet with him, but His saying: ﴿So say, "Indeed we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds"﴾ indicates it.

As for His saying: ﴿And they have a charge against me﴾, by the charge he meant his killing of the Copt. God, the Exalted, has recounted this story in detail in Surah al-Qasas.

Know that in Musa's request, peace be upon him, that Harun be joined with him, there is nothing indicating that he sought to be excused from going to Fir'awn. Rather, his aim in what he asked was that this going should take place in the best manner for reaching the goal. The scholars differed. Some said: although he was a prophet, he did not know that he would remain alive until he delivered the message, because he was only commanded to do so on condition of being enabled. This is the view of al-Ka'bi and others among the Baghdadis, because they permit the condition to enter into God's imposition of obligation (taklif) upon the servant. What the majority held is that this is not permissible, because when God, the Exalted, commands, He knows what the one commanded is able to do and the times of his ability. If He knows that he is not able to do it, He does not command him to do it. Given this, the more probable view regarding the prophets is that when God, the Exalted, entrusts them with the message, they know that God will enable them to deliver it and that they will remain until that time. Such a thing does not constitute inducement to sin (ighra') in the case of prophets, although it may constitute inducement to sin in the case of others.

**The third question:** One might say: Does Musa's saying, peace be upon him, ﴿And they have a charge against me﴾ indicate that he committed a sin?

The answer: No. What is meant is: they have a charge against me in their claim.

The second: that He would send Aaron along with him.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿Indeed We are with you, listening﴾, it is a figurative expression (majāz, a non-literal usage). It means: "We are for you both and against your enemy, like a helper and supporter for you against him. We will be present and listen to what passes between you, and so We will make you prevail over him, exalt you, and break his power over you." We took "listening" as figurative because listening is an expression for giving attention, and that is impossible for God the Exalted.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿Indeed we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾, there is a question about it: why was "messenger" not put in the dual, as it was in His saying ﴿Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40]? The answer is given in several ways:

First: "messenger" is a term for the quiddity (māhiyya, the essence or nature) without indicating whether that quiddity is one or many, and the definite article (al-) only indicates unity, not totality. The proof is that you say, "Man is the laugher," but you do not say, "Every man is the laugher," nor "This man is the laugher." Since it is established that the word "messenger" indicates only the quiddity, and that the quiddity may be applied to one or to two, the correctness of His saying ﴿Indeed we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ is established.

Second: "messenger" may mean "message" (risāla). The poet said:

"The slanderers have lied; I did not divulge a secret to them, nor did I send them as a messenger (rasūl)."

So the meaning is: "Indeed we are possessors of the message of the Lord of the worlds."

Third: because the two of them agreed upon one law and were united through the bond of brotherhood, they were as if they were one messenger.

Fourth: the intended meaning is that each one of us is a messenger.

Fifth: what some of them have said: he said it without the dual form because he was the messenger in particular, and His saying ﴿Indeed we﴾ is like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed We sent it down﴾. This view is weak.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿that you send with us the Children of Israel﴾, the meaning of this "sending" is release and freedom, like your saying, "Send the falcon," meaning: let them go to go with us.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 26, verses 21–23:

﴿He said: "I did it then, when I was of those astray."﴾ ﴿So I fled from you when I feared you, and my Lord granted me wisdom and made me one of the messengers.﴾ ﴿And is this a favour you count against me, that you have enslaved the Children of Israel?﴾

Know that when Pharaoh mentioned the upbringing and mentioned the killing, and his upbringing of Moses was well known and evident, Moses, peace be upon him, did not deny it and did not occupy himself with answering it. This is because it is established in the minds that when a messenger is sent to others and has with him a miracle (mu'jiz) and a proof (hujjah), his standing does not change by whether the one he is sent to has bestowed a favour on him or not. So Pharaoh's statement, having been said, had no effect whatsoever, and turning away from such speech is more fitting. However, he answered regarding the killing with the most eloquent answer possible, which is his saying: ﴿I did it then, when I was of those astray.﴾ By "those astray" is meant those heedless of knowing what the killing would lead to, because he struck the blow as a form of discipline, and such a thing may sometimes be good even if it leads to death. So he made clear to him that he did it in a manner that does not allow him to be held accountable for it, nor to be counted as a disbeliever, or as one ungrateful for his blessings.

As for his saying: ﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾, the meaning is that I did that deed while I was heedless of its being fatal, and it was, on my part, in the category of inadvertence. Therefore I did not deserve the threat that necessitates flight. Yet even so, I fled from you when you said: ﴿Indeed, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you﴾ [al-Qasas: 20]. Thereby he made clear that Pharaoh had no favour upon him in the matter of that deed; rather, being at fault in it is closer, since he was threatened with a threat that necessitated flight. Then he mentioned God Most High's blessing upon him after the flight, as if he were saying: You have done wrong, and God has done good to me by granting me wisdom and making me one of the messengers.

Scholars differed about the "wisdom" (hukm). The closer view is that it is other than prophethood, because the conjoined is different from that to which it is conjoined, and prophethood is understood from his saying: ﴿and made me one of the messengers﴾. Therefore, by "wisdom" is meant knowledge, and included in knowledge are intellect, sound judgement, and knowledge of the religion, which is monotheism (tawhid). This is the closer view, because God Most High would not send him except with his perfection in intellect, judgement, and knowledge of monotheism. And his saying: ﴿So my Lord granted me wisdom﴾

[Page 110]

is like an explicit statement that this wisdom is among the creations of God Most High. The Mu'tazilites (al-Mu'tazilah, a rationalist theological school) said: what is meant by it is the divine favours (al-altaf), but this is very weak, because the divine favours are granted to all without deficiency or shortcoming, so specification must have a benefit in it.

As for his saying: ﴿And is this a favour you count against me, that you have enslaved the Children of Israel?﴾, it is an answer to his saying: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾ It is said: "I enslaved the man" (ʿabbadtu al-rajul) and "I made him a slave" (aʿbadtuhu) when one takes him as a slave. If it is asked: how can that be an answer to his statement when there is no connection between the two matters? We say: the connection is shown in several ways:

First: his upbringing happened in his hand and under his care only because he intended to enslave the Children of Israel and slaughter their sons. So it is as if he, peace be upon him, said to him: "I would have been independent of your upbringing had there not been from you that prior injustice upon us and upon our forefathers."

Second: this later favour is counterbalanced by that great injustice upon our forefathers, and when two things are counterbalanced, they cancel each other out.

Third: what al-Hasan said: "You enslaved them and took their wealth, and from it you spent upon me, so there is no favour to you by the upbringing."

Fourth: the meaning is that those who undertook my upbringing were those whom you had enslaved, so there is no favour from you upon me, because the upbringing came from my mother and the rest of my people. What you have is only that you did not kill me, and such a thing is not counted as a favour.

Fifth: you used to claim that the Children of Israel were your slaves, and there is no obligation of the master upon the slave in that he feeds him and gives him what he needs.

Know that in the verse there is evidence that a disbeliever's disbelief does not nullify his favour upon one to whom he does good, nor does it nullify his obligation, because Moses, peace be upon him, only nullified that by another way, as we have explained. The scholars differed. Some of them said: if he is a disbeliever, he does not deserve thanks for his favours upon people; he deserves only humiliation because of his disbelief. So if he deserved thanks for his beneficence, and thanks is not found except with honour, then it follows that he deserves both humiliation and honour together, and deserving the combination of two opposites is impossible. Others said: thanks is not nullified by disbelief; rather, what disbelief nullifies is the reward and the praise that he deserves for faith. The verse indicates this second view.

Second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: the pronoun was made plural in "minkum" and "khiftukum" along with its being singular in "tamunnuha" and "ʿabbadta" because the fear and the flight did not come from him alone, but from him and from his chiefs who were conspiring to kill him, as evidenced by his saying: ﴿Indeed, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you﴾. As for the bestowing of favour (imtinan), it is from him alone, and likewise the enslaving. If you say: to what does "tilka" (that) refer, and what is the grammatical position (i'rab) of ﴿an ʿabbadta﴾? I say: "tilka" refers to a shameful, vague matter, which is not known what it is except by its explanation, and it is ﴿an ʿabbadta﴾. So ﴿an ʿabbadta﴾ is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan), and its parallel is his saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We decreed to him that matter, that the root of these will be cut off by morning﴾ [al-Hijr: 66]. The meaning is: your enslaving of the Children of Israel is a favour you count against me. Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible that "an" be in the accusative position, and the meaning is: it became a favour upon me only because you enslaved the Children of Israel, that is, if you had not done that, my own family would have sufficed me.

However, he answered regarding the killing with the most eloquent answer possible, which is his saying: ﴿I did it then, when I was of those astray.﴾ By "those astray" is meant those heedless of knowing what the killing would lead to, because he struck the blow as a form of discipline, and such a thing may sometimes be good even if it leads to death. So he made clear to him that he did it in a manner that does not allow him to be held accountable for it, nor to be counted as a disbeliever, or as one ungrateful for his blessings.

As for his saying: ﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾, the meaning is that I did that deed while I was heedless of its being fatal, and it was, on my part, in the category of inadvertence. Therefore I did not deserve the threat that necessitates flight. Yet even so, I fled from you when you said: ﴿Indeed, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you﴾ [al-Qasas: 20]. Thereby he made clear that Pharaoh had no favour upon him in the matter of that deed; rather, being at fault in it is closer, since he was threatened with a threat that necessitated flight. Then he mentioned God Most High's blessing upon him after the flight, as if he were saying: You have done wrong, and God has done good to me by granting me wisdom and making me one of the messengers.

Scholars differed about the "wisdom" (hukm). The closer view is that it is other than prophethood, because the conjoined is different from that to which it is conjoined, and prophethood is understood from his saying: ﴿and made me one of the messengers﴾. Therefore, by "wisdom" is meant knowledge, and included in knowledge are intellect, sound judgement, and knowledge of the religion, which is monotheism (tawhid). This is the closer view, because God Most High would not send him except with his perfection in intellect, judgement, and knowledge of monotheism. And his saying: ﴿So my Lord granted me wisdom﴾

[Page 110]

is like an explicit statement that this wisdom is among the creations of God Most High. The Mu'tazilites (al-Mu'tazilah, a rationalist theological school) said: what is meant by it is the divine favours (al-altaf), but this is very weak, because the divine favours are granted to all without deficiency or shortcoming, so specification must have a benefit in it.

As for his saying: ﴿And is this a favour you count against me, that you have enslaved the Children of Israel?﴾, it is an answer to his saying: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾ It is said: "I enslaved the man" (ʿabbadtu al-rajul) and "I made him a slave" (aʿbadtuhu) when one takes him as a slave. If it is asked: how can that be an answer to his statement when there is no connection between the two matters? We say: the connection is shown in several ways:

First: his upbringing happened in his hand and under his care only because he intended to enslave the Children of Israel and slaughter their sons. So it is as if he, peace be upon him, said to him: "I would have been independent of your upbringing had there not been from you that prior injustice upon us and upon our forefathers."

Second: this later favour is counterbalanced by that great injustice upon our forefathers, and when two things are counterbalanced, they cancel each other out.

Third: what al-Hasan said: "You enslaved them and took their wealth, and from it you spent upon me, so there is no favour to you by the upbringing."

Fourth: the meaning is that those who undertook my upbringing were those whom you had enslaved, so there is no favour from you upon me, because the upbringing came from my mother and the rest of my people. What you have is only that you did not kill me, and such a thing is not counted as a favour.

Fifth: you used to claim that the Children of Israel were your slaves, and there is no obligation of the master upon the slave in that he feeds him and gives him what he needs.

Know that in the verse there is evidence that a disbeliever's disbelief does not nullify his favour upon one to whom he does good, nor does it nullify his obligation, because Moses, peace be upon him, only nullified that by another way, as we have explained. The scholars differed. Some of them said: if he is a disbeliever, he does not deserve thanks for his favours upon people; he deserves only humiliation because of his disbelief. So if he deserved thanks for his beneficence, and thanks is not found except with honour, then it follows that he deserves both humiliation and honour together, and deserving the combination of two opposites is impossible. Others said: thanks is not nullified by disbelief; rather, what disbelief nullifies is the reward and the praise that he deserves for faith. The verse indicates this second view.

Second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: the pronoun was made plural in "minkum" and "khiftukum" along with its being singular in "tamunnuha" and "ʿabbadta" because the fear and the flight did not come from him alone, but from him and from his chiefs who were conspiring to kill him, as evidenced by his saying: ﴿Indeed, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you﴾. As for the bestowing of favour (imtinan), it is from him alone, and likewise the enslaving. If you say: to what does "tilka" (that) refer, and what is the grammatical position (i'rab) of ﴿an ʿabbadta﴾? I say: "tilka" refers to a shameful, vague matter, which is not known what it is except by its explanation, and it is ﴿an ʿabbadta﴾. So ﴿an ʿabbadta﴾ is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan), and its parallel is his saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We decreed to him that matter, that the root of these will be cut off by morning﴾ [al-Hijr: 66]. The meaning is: your enslaving of the Children of Israel is a favour you count against me. Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible that "an" be in the accusative position, and the meaning is: it became a favour upon me only because you enslaved the Children of Israel, that is, if you had not done that, my own family would have sufficed me.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Pharaoh said, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?"﴾ ﴿[Moses] said, "The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you are certain."﴾ ﴿He said to those around him, "Do you not listen?"﴾ ﴿[Moses] said, "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones."﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad."﴾ ﴿[Moses] said, "The Lord of the east and the west and whatever is between them, if you use your reason."﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned."﴾ ﴿[Moses] said, "Even if I bring you something clear?"﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "Then bring it, if you are of the truthful."﴾

Know that Pharaoh did not say to Moses, ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ except that Moses had called him to obey the Lord of the worlds. This is shown by what preceded it, His saying: ﴿So go to Pharaoh and say, "Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds."﴾ Therefore, when the two of them entered upon him, they must have said that, and so Pharaoh said, ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ Then there are two discussions here.

The first discussion: It may be said that Pharaoh was a knower of God, but he said what he said seeking kingship and leadership. Allah the Exalted has mentioned in His Book what indicates that he was a knower of God, namely His saying: ﴿[Moses] said, "You certainly know that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth"﴾ [al-Isra: 102]. When the verb ﴿you know﴾ is read with a fatha on the ta' (ʿalimta), the meaning is that Pharaoh knew this, and that indicates he was a knower of God, but he was using his claimed divinity to deceive and exploit his people. The other reading is with a damma on the ta' (ʿalimtu), which requires that it was Moses, peace be upon him, who knew this. Also, if Pharaoh were not rational, it would not be permissible for Allah the Exalted to send a messenger to him. And if he was rational, he would know by necessity that he had not existed, nor been living, nor rational, and then became so. And by necessity he knows that everything that is like this must have a cause. Thus there must arise in him from these two knowledges a third knowledge: that in his composition, his life, and his reason he needs an originating cause. It may also be said that he followed the doctrine of the Dahriyya (materialist naturalists), who held that the spheres (al-aflak) are necessary in their own essence (wajib al-wujud, the Necessary Existent, that which must exist) and move by their own essence, and that their motions are the causes for the occurrence of events in this world. Or it may be said that he was one of the philosophers who believed in a necessitating cause rather than a free chooser, and then he believed that he was in the position of a god for the people of his land, inasmuch as he enslaved them, possessed their protection, and held the reins of their affairs. It may also be said that he followed the doctrine of the Hulūliyya (Incarnationists), who hold that the essence of God clothes itself in the body of a specific human being, so that God, glorified is He, stands to that body as the soul of each person stands to his body. On these assumptions, he called himself a god.

The second discussion: He said to Moses, peace be upon him, ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ Know that a question with "what" (mā) seeks to define the reality of a thing. Defining the reality of a thing is either by that reality itself, or by some part of it, or by something external to it, or by what is composed of the internal and the external. As for defining it by itself, that is impossible, because the defined must be known before the defining; so if one defined a thing by itself, it would follow that it is known before it is known, which is absurd. As for defining it by the things included within it, that is impossible here with respect to the Necessary Existent, because definition by constituent parts is only possible when the thing defined is composite, and the Necessary Existent is impossible to be composite. For every composite is in need of each of its parts, and each of its parts is other than it, so every composite is in need of something other than itself, and whatever is in need of something other than itself is contingent in its essence (mumkin, the contingent). Every composite is contingent, so whatever is not contingent is impossible to be composite. Therefore the Necessary Existent is not composite, and when it is not composite, it is impossible to define it by its parts. Since these two divisions have been shown to be invalid, it is established that the quiddity (māhiyya, what-it-is-ness) of the Necessary Existent cannot be defined except by its necessary consequences and its effects. Then the necessary consequences may be hidden or evident. It is not permissible to define a quiddity by hidden necessary consequences; rather, it must be defined by evident necessary consequences. The most manifest effect of the essence of the Necessary Existent is this sensible world, namely the heavens

[p. 112]

and the earth and whatever is between them. It is thus established that there is absolutely no answer to Pharaoh's saying ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ except what Moses, peace be upon him, said, namely that He is ﴿the Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them.﴾ As for his saying ﴿if you are certain,﴾ its meaning is: if you are certain that these sensible things are ascribed to a being that is Necessary Existent, then know that He cannot be defined except by what I have mentioned. For since you have conceded that these sensible things terminate in that which is Necessary by its own essence, it is established that the Necessary by its essence is a absolute unity (fard muṭlaq), and it is established that an absolute unity cannot be defined except by its effects, and it is established that those effects must be its most manifest effects and the furthest from concealment, and that is nothing but the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them. So if you are certain of this, it must follow for you that you conclude there is no answer to that question except this answer. When Moses, peace be upon him, gave this true answer, Pharaoh said, ﴿to those around him, "Do you not listen?"﴾ He said this by way of astonishment at Moses' answer, meaning: I ask him for the quiddity and the particular reality, and he answers me with agency and causation. The full difficulty is that defining a quiddity by its necessary consequences does not yield knowledge of that quiddity itself. For when we say of a thing that it is that which has such-and-such necessary consequence, this thing mentioned is known either merely by being something that has that consequence, or by the particularity of that quiddity to which this necessary relation has attached. The first is impossible, because its being something that has that necessary consequence is what we made the revealing factor; so if what is revealed were only this much, it would follow that a thing is known by itself, which is impossible. The second is also impossible, because knowing that it is something that has such-and-such necessary consequence does not yield knowledge of the particularity of that necessitated quiddity, since in the intellect it is not impossible for different quiddities to share equal necessary consequences. Thus it is established that definition by an external attribute does not yield knowledge of the essence of the reality. Therefore, his being Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them was not an answer to his question ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ So Moses, peace be upon him, answered by saying ﴿"Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones."﴾ It is as though he shifted from defining by the creatorship of the heaven and the earth to defining by His being the creator of us and our forefathers. This is because it is not impossible that someone might believe the heavens and the earths are necessary in their essence, and so they are independent of a creator and originator; but a sensible person cannot believe that himself, his father, and his grandfathers are necessary in their essence, because observation shows that they came into existence after non-existence and then ceased to exist after existence; and whatever is like this is impossible to be necessary in its essence, and whatever is not necessary in its essence is impossible to exist except through a cause. So definition through this effect was more evident, and for this reason Moses, peace be upon him, shifted from the first statement to it. Then Pharaoh said, ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad.﴾ He means: the purpose of the question is seeking the quiddity and the particularity of the reality, and definition through these external effects does not at all yield that particularity. Therefore this one who claims to be a messenger is mad, not understanding the question, let alone being able to answer it. Then Moses, peace be upon him, said, ﴿The Lord of the east and the west and whatever is between them, if you use your reason.﴾ So he turned to a third way, clearer than the second. This is because by "the east" he meant the rising of the sun and the appearance of daylight, and by "the west" the setting of the sun and the passing of daylight. The matter is evident that this constant arrangement, in this wondrous form, cannot be accomplished except by an arranger. This is exactly the method of Abraham, peace be upon him, with Nimrod, for he first argued from giving life and causing death, which is what Moses, peace be upon him, mentioned here with his saying ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones.﴾ Nimrod answered him with his saying ﴿"I give life and cause death,"﴾ [al-Baqara: 258]. Then he said ﴿"Indeed, God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." Thus the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾ [al-Baqara: 258]. This is what Moses, peace be upon him, mentioned here with his saying ﴿The Lord of the east and the west.﴾

* * *

As for his saying ﴿if you use your reason,﴾ it is as though he, peace be upon him, said: If you are among the sensible, you know that there is no answer to your question except what you have mentioned, because you asked me to define its reality

[p. 113]

neither by its own reality nor by the parts of its reality. So nothing remains except that I define its reality by the effects of its reality, and I have defined its reality by the effects of its reality. Thus it is established that everyone who is sensible concludes that there is no answer to this question except what I have mentioned.

Know that we explained in Surat al-An'am, in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am: 18], that the reality of God, glorified is He, in itself is not comprehensible to human beings. Since this is so, it is impossible for Moses, peace be upon him, to mention that by which that reality is known. Yet the lack of knowledge of that particularity does not impair the validity of the prophethood. Thus the sum of Moses' speech, peace be upon him, is that the claim to be a messenger of the Lord of the worlds depends for its validity on establishing that the worlds have a lord and god, and does not depend on knowing the particularity of the Lord, exalted is He, and His specific quiddity. So Moses, peace be upon him, establishes the proof for the amount needed for the validity of the claim to prophethood, while Pharaoh demands an explanation of the quiddity. Moses, peace be upon him, was turning away from that question, knowing that this question has no bearing, neither in negation nor affirmation, on what is sought. This is the full account of this discussion, and Allah knows best.

Then, when Moses, peace be upon him, became harsh at the end of his speech with his saying ﴿if you use your reason,﴾ Pharaoh said at that point, ﴿"If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned."﴾ For when he was unable to argue, he turned to intimidation. At that point Moses, peace be upon him, said an ambiguous statement so that his heart would be attached to it and he would turn away from his threat, and he said ﴿"Even if I bring you something clear?"﴾ That is, do you consider it permissible to imprison me while I am capable of bringing you a matter clear in demonstrating the existence of Allah the Exalted and that I am His messenger? At that point he said ﴿"Then bring it, if you are of the truthful."﴾ Here there are several branches.

The first branch: The verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is not a body, for if He were a body with a form, Moses' answer would have been by mentioning His reality, and Pharaoh's speech would have been pertinent to Him, since he deviated from the true answer.

The second: It is obligatory upon one who calls others to Allah the Exalted not to answer foolishness, for when Pharaoh said to him that he was mad, Moses did not turn away from mentioning the proof; and likewise when he threatened to imprison him.

The third: It is permissible for the one being questioned to shift in his argument from one example to another to clarify the speech, and that does not indicate an inability to respond.

The fourth: If it is asked, how did he cut off the speech with something unrelated to the first, namely his saying ﴿"Even if I bring you something clear?"﴾ and the miracle does not indicate Allah the Exalted in the way that all that preceded does? We answer: Rather, what he intended to display, namely the transformation of the staff into a serpent, indicates Allah the Exalted and His oneness, and that he is truthful in the prophethood. So what he concluded his speech with is stronger than and more comprehensive than everything that preceded.

**Fifth:** If it is asked, how did he say ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ in the dual, when the thing referred to is plural? The answer: what is meant is what lies between the two directions (the two sides). If it is asked, mentioning the heavens and the earth and what is between them has already encompassed all creatures, so what is the point of mentioning the people and their fathers after that, and mentioning the east and the west? The answer: he first generalized, then singled out from the general, for clarification, themselves and their fathers, because the things closest to a rational person are himself, those born from him, and what he has witnessed of his own transition, from the time of his birth to the time of his death, from one state to another. Then he singled out the east and the west, because the rising of the sun from one of the two horizons and its setting, on a regular course through the seasons of the year, are among the clearest signs.

**Sixth:** If it is asked why he said ﴿I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾ and did not say "I will surely imprison you," even though the latter is shorter? The answer: had he said "I will imprison you," it would only convey that he would become a prisoner. But ﴿I will make you among the imprisoned﴾ means: I will make you one of those whose condition you have come to know in my prisons. It was his custom to take whoever he wished to imprison and throw him alone into a deep well, where he could neither see nor hear, and this was harsher than killing.

**Seventh:** The *wāw* in ﴿Even if I bring you﴾ is the *wāw* of circumstance (*wāw al-ḥāl*), into which the interrogative *hamza* (*hamzat al-istifhām*) has entered. Its meaning is: "Will you do this to me even if I bring you something clear?" That is, coming to you with a miracle.

The full difficulty is that defining a quiddity by its necessary consequences does not yield knowledge of that quiddity itself. For when we say of a thing that it is that which has such-and-such necessary consequence, this thing mentioned is known either merely by being something that has that consequence, or by the particularity of that quiddity to which this necessary relation has attached. The first is impossible, because its being something that has that necessary consequence is what we made the revealing factor; so if what is revealed were only this much, it would follow that a thing is known by itself, which is impossible. The second is also impossible, because knowing that it is something that has such-and-such necessary consequence does not yield knowledge of the particularity of that necessitated quiddity, since in the intellect it is not impossible for different quiddities to share equal necessary consequences. Thus it is established that definition by an external attribute does not yield knowledge of the essence of the reality. Therefore, his being Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them was not an answer to his question ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ So Moses, peace be upon him, answered by saying ﴿"Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones."﴾ It is as though he shifted from defining by the creatorship of the heaven and the earth to defining by His being the creator of us and our forefathers. This is because it is not impossible that someone might believe the heavens and the earths are necessary in their essence, and so they are independent of a creator and originator; but a sensible person cannot believe that himself, his father, and his grandfathers are necessary in their essence, because observation shows that they came into existence after non-existence and then ceased to exist after existence; and whatever is like this is impossible to be necessary in its essence, and whatever is not necessary in its essence is impossible to exist except through a cause. So definition through this effect was more evident, and for this reason Moses, peace be upon him, shifted from the first statement to it. Then Pharaoh said, ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad.﴾ He means: the purpose of the question is seeking the quiddity and the particularity of the reality, and definition through these external effects does not at all yield that particularity. Therefore this one who claims to be a messenger is mad, not understanding the question, let alone being able to answer it. Then Moses, peace be upon him, said, ﴿The Lord of the east and the west and whatever is between them, if you use your reason.﴾ So he turned to a third way, clearer than the second. This is because by "the east" he meant the rising of the sun and the appearance of daylight, and by "the west" the setting of the sun and the passing of daylight. The matter is evident that this constant arrangement, in this wondrous form, cannot be accomplished except by an arranger. This is exactly the method of Abraham, peace be upon him, with Nimrod, for he first argued from giving life and causing death, which is what Moses, peace be upon him, mentioned here with his saying ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones.﴾ Nimrod answered him with his saying ﴿"I give life and cause death,"﴾ [al-Baqara: 258]. Then he said ﴿"Indeed, God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." Thus the one who disbelieved was confounded﴾ [al-Baqara: 258]. This is what Moses, peace be upon him, mentioned here with his saying ﴿The Lord of the east and the west.﴾

* * *

As for his saying ﴿if you use your reason,﴾ it is as though he, peace be upon him, said: If you are among the sensible, you know that there is no answer to your question except what you have mentioned, because you asked me to define its reality

[p. 113]

neither by its own reality nor by the parts of its reality. So nothing remains except that I define its reality by the effects of its reality, and I have defined its reality by the effects of its reality. Thus it is established that everyone who is sensible concludes that there is no answer to this question except what I have mentioned.

Know that we explained in Surat al-An'am, in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ [al-An'am: 18], that the reality of God, glorified is He, in itself is not comprehensible to human beings. Since this is so, it is impossible for Moses, peace be upon him, to mention that by which that reality is known. Yet the lack of knowledge of that particularity does not impair the validity of the prophethood. Thus the sum of Moses' speech, peace be upon him, is that the claim to be a messenger of the Lord of the worlds depends for its validity on establishing that the worlds have a lord and god, and does not depend on knowing the particularity of the Lord, exalted is He, and His specific quiddity. So Moses, peace be upon him, establishes the proof for the amount needed for the validity of the claim to prophethood, while Pharaoh demands an explanation of the quiddity. Moses, peace be upon him, was turning away from that question, knowing that this question has no bearing, neither in negation nor affirmation, on what is sought. This is the full account of this discussion, and Allah knows best.

Then, when Moses, peace be upon him, became harsh at the end of his speech with his saying ﴿if you use your reason,﴾ Pharaoh said at that point, ﴿"If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned."﴾ For when he was unable to argue, he turned to intimidation. At that point Moses, peace be upon him, said an ambiguous statement so that his heart would be attached to it and he would turn away from his threat, and he said ﴿"Even if I bring you something clear?"﴾ That is, do you consider it permissible to imprison me while I am capable of bringing you a matter clear in demonstrating the existence of Allah the Exalted and that I am His messenger? At that point he said ﴿"Then bring it, if you are of the truthful."﴾ Here there are several branches.

The first branch: The verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is not a body, for if He were a body with a form, Moses' answer would have been by mentioning His reality, and Pharaoh's speech would have been pertinent to Him, since he deviated from the true answer.

The second: It is obligatory upon one who calls others to Allah the Exalted not to answer foolishness, for when Pharaoh said to him that he was mad, Moses did not turn away from mentioning the proof; and likewise when he threatened to imprison him.

The third: It is permissible for the one being questioned to shift in his argument from one example to another to clarify the speech, and that does not indicate an inability to respond.

The fourth: If it is asked, how did he cut off the speech with something unrelated to the first, namely his saying ﴿"Even if I bring you something clear?"﴾ and the miracle does not indicate Allah the Exalted in the way that all that preceded does? We answer: Rather, what he intended to display, namely the transformation of the staff into a serpent, indicates Allah the Exalted and His oneness, and that he is truthful in the prophethood. So what he concluded his speech with is stronger than and more comprehensive than everything that preceded.

**Fifth:** If it is asked, how did he say ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ in the dual, when the thing referred to is plural? The answer: what is meant is what lies between the two directions (the two sides). If it is asked, mentioning the heavens and the earth and what is between them has already encompassed all creatures, so what is the point of mentioning the people and their fathers after that, and mentioning the east and the west? The answer: he first generalized, then singled out from the general, for clarification, themselves and their fathers, because the things closest to a rational person are himself, those born from him, and what he has witnessed of his own transition, from the time of his birth to the time of his death, from one state to another. Then he singled out the east and the west, because the rising of the sun from one of the two horizons and its setting, on a regular course through the seasons of the year, are among the clearest signs.

**Sixth:** If it is asked why he said ﴿I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾ and did not say "I will surely imprison you," even though the latter is shorter? The answer: had he said "I will imprison you," it would only convey that he would become a prisoner. But ﴿I will make you among the imprisoned﴾ means: I will make you one of those whose condition you have come to know in my prisons. It was his custom to take whoever he wished to imprison and throw him alone into a deep well, where he could neither see nor hear, and this was harsher than killing.

**Seventh:** The *wāw* in ﴿Even if I bring you﴾ is the *wāw* of circumstance (*wāw al-ḥāl*), into which the interrogative *hamza* (*hamzat al-istifhām*) has entered. Its meaning is: "Will you do this to me even if I bring you something clear?" That is, coming to you with a miracle.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 26, verses 34–37:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent.﴾ ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers.﴾ ﴿He said to the eminent ones around him, "Indeed this is a knowing sorcerer.﴾ ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land with his magic, so what do you advise?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Put him off, and his brother, and send heralds to the cities﴾ ﴿to bring you every knowing sorcerer."﴾

And in it are several issues:

The first issue: al-A'mash recited: "bikulli saahirin 'aleem" (every sorcerer, knowing).

The second issue: Know that His saying, ﴿Even if I bring you something clear?﴾ (Q 26:30) indicates that God, exalted is He, informed Moses, before he threw the staff, that He would turn it into a serpent; otherwise he would not have said what he said. So when he threw his staff, what God had promised him appeared, and it became a manifest serpent. The meaning is that it became clear to the onlookers that it was a serpent, by its movements and all the other signs. It is narrated that when it turned into a snake, it rose into the sky about a mile, then descended toward Pharaoh, coming forward, and began to say: "O Moses, command me with whatever you wish." And Pharaoh said: "O Moses, I ask you by the One who sent you, will you not take it?" So it returned to being a staff.

If it is asked: Why did He say here, ﴿a clearly visible serpent﴾, while in another verse it is: ﴿and behold, it was a snake, moving swiftly﴾ (Q 20:20), and in a third verse: ﴿as if it were a jinn﴾ (Q 27:10), and the jinn tends toward smallness while the serpent tends toward largeness?

Its answer: As for the snake (ḥayya), it is a generic noun; then, because of its largeness, it became a serpent (thuʿbān). He likened it to a jinn because of its lightness and swiftness, so both statements are correct. It is also possible that He likened it to a devil, based on His saying: ﴿And the jinn We had created before from the fire of scorching wind﴾ (Q 15:27). It is also possible that it was initially small, like a jinn, and then grew large and became a serpent.

Then, when Moses, peace be upon him, brought this sign, Pharaoh said to him: "Is there anything other than this?" He said: "Yes," and he showed him his hand, then put it into his pocket and drew it out, and behold, it was white, shining over the valley because of its intense whiteness, without any leprosy, having a ray like the ray of the sun. At this point Pharaoh wanted to conceal this proof from his people, so he mentioned in it three matters:

The first: his saying: ﴿Indeed this is a knowing sorcerer.﴾ This is because the era was an era of sorcerers, and it was held by many of them that a sorcerer may possibly reach this degree with his magic; therefore he made this statement appealing to them.

The second: his saying: ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land with his magic.﴾ This operates as a means of repelling them from him, so that they would not accept his words. The meaning is: he wants to drive you out of your land by what he casts among you of enmities, so that he divides your assembly. And it is known that leaving one's homeland is among the most difficult of matters, so he repelled them from him by this. This is the utmost that the falsifier does in repelling people from the one who is right.

The third: his saying to them: ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ That is, what is your opinion regarding him, and what should I do? He shows himself to be one who follows your opinion and submits to your word. Such speech draws hearts and turns them away from the enemy. So at these words they agreed upon a single answer, which is his saying: ﴿Put him off.﴾ It was read "arjiʾhu" and "arjihu," with hamza and without hamza; both are dialects, and it is said: arjaʾtuhu and arjaytuhu, meaning "I delayed him." The meaning is: delay him and his debate until the time of the gathering of the sorcerers. It is also said: "Hold him back," which is possible, because when you detain a man from his need, you have delayed him. It is narrated that Pharaoh wanted to kill him but could not reach him, so they said to him: "Do not do it, for if you kill him you will introduce doubt among the people about his matter. Rather, put him off and his brother until you gather the sorcerers to oppose him, so that no proof will stand for him against you." Then they advised him to dispatch heralds who would gather

the sorcerers, supposing that if they overcame him, they would expose his condition and counter his words: ﴿Indeed this is a knowing sorcerer﴾ by their saying: ﴿every knowing sorcerer.﴾ So they came with the word of comprehensiveness and the form of intensification, in order to console his heart and calm some of his anxiety. I say: it is in the accusative in two ways: accusative in form and accusative in position. The governing element for the formal accusative is what is implied in the adverb of place, and the governing element for the positional accusative is that it is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl).

The author of al-Kashshaf said: If you say, regarding His saying, ﴿He said to the eminent ones around him,﴾ what is the governing element in "ḥawlahu" (around him)? I say: it is in the accusative in two ways: accusative in form and accusative in position. The governing element for the formal accusative is what is implied in the adverb of place, and the governing element for the positional accusative is that it is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 26, verse 38–42:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So the magicians were assembled for the appointed time of a known day﴾ ﴿And it was said to the people, "Are you assembling?"﴾ ﴿"That we may follow the magicians, if they are the victors."﴾ ﴿So when the magicians came, they said to Pharaoh, "Indeed, will there be a reward for us if we are the victors?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Yes, and indeed you will be, in that case, among the near ones."﴾.

In it are two issues:

The first issue: The known day is the Day of Adornment (yawm al-zinah), and its appointed time (miqat) is the time of forenoon (waqt al-duha), because it is the time that Musa, peace be upon him, set for them on the Day of Adornment, in his saying: ﴿Your appointment is the Day of Adornment, and let the people be gathered at forenoon﴾ [Taha: 59]. The miqat (appointed time, technical term meaning a time or place fixed for an act of worship or meeting) is that by which something is set, i.e., determined as to place and time; and from it come the mawaqit al-ihram (the fixed places of assuming the state of ihram).

The second issue: Know that when the people advised delaying his matter and gathering the magicians for him, so that the corruption of Musa's peace be upon him saying would become apparent at their presence, Pharaoh agreed to what they had said and became blind to what he had witnessed, and love of a thing blinds and deafens. So he gathered the magicians, then wished that that debate take place on a day of their festival, so that it would be in the presence of the great multitude. Musa, peace be upon him, was seeking that, so that his proof would become manifest to them before the great multitude. This was also one of the kindnesses of God, exalted is He, in the manifestation of the matter of Musa, peace be upon him.

As for His saying: ﴿And it was said to the people, "Are you assembling?"﴾, the meaning is that they were sent forth to attend, so that they might witness what would happen from both sides.

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿"That we may follow the magicians"﴾, the meaning is that we hope the victory will be theirs, so we will follow them. Then, when the magicians came, they began by asking for the reward, which was either wealth or rank, so he granted them that and confirmed it with his saying: ﴿"Indeed, you will be, in that case, among the near ones."﴾, because the ultimate of their aim from him was giving and elevation of station, so he granted both matters.

[Page 116]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Moses said to them, "Throw what you are going to throw."﴾ ﴿So they threw their ropes and their staffs and said, "By the might of Pharaoh, indeed we will be the victorious."﴾ ﴿Then Moses threw his staff, and suddenly it devoured what they had falsely presented.﴾ ﴿So the magicians fell down in prostration.﴾ ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron."﴾

Know that when they gathered, it was necessary that either Moses would begin or they would begin. Then they showed humility toward him and put him before themselves, and they said: ﴿Either you throw first, or we will be the first to throw﴾ [Ta-Ha: 65]. When they showed humility toward him, he also showed humility toward them and put them before himself, and said: ﴿Throw what you are going to throw.﴾ If it is asked: how was it permissible for Moses, peace be upon him, to command the magicians to throw the ropes and staffs, when that is magic, deception and disbelief, and commanding the like of it is not permissible? The answer: there is no doubt that this was not a command, because what Moses, peace be upon him, intended from them was that they believe in him and not proceed to what amounts to a contest. Once this is established, the form of the command must be interpreted, and there are several ways to do so:

The first: that command was conditional, and the meaning is: "Throw what you are going to throw, if you are truthful," as in His saying: ﴿So bring a surah like it and call upon your witnesses other than Allah, if you are truthful﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 23].

The second: once that became the means to removing the doubt, it became permissible.

The third: that this is not a command but a threat, meaning: "If you do that, we will bring what nullifies it," like the saying of one who says: "If you shoot at me, I will certainly do such-and-such and such-and-such," and then he sets the arrow on the string and says to him, "Shoot," and that is from him a threat.

The fourth: what we mentioned, that when they showed humility toward him and put him before themselves, he put them before himself in hope that this humility would be a cause for accepting the truth. Indeed, by the blessing of that humility, that desired outcome was achieved. This is an alert that what befits the Muslim in all circumstances is humility, because if someone like Moses, peace be upon him, did not abandon humility even with those magicians, then it is more fitting that one of us do so.

Regarding His words, ﴿So they cast down their ropes and their staffs﴾: it is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that when they cast down their ropes and their staffs, and the ropes had been smeared with mercury and the staffs were hollow and filled with mercury, then when they were heated their movement intensified, so they became like serpents crawling from every side of the ground. Moses, peace be upon him, was frightened by that, so it was said to him: ﴿Cast down what is in your right hand.﴾ ﴿So he cast down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent.﴾ Then it opened its mouth and swallowed all that they had thrown of their ropes and staffs, until it had devoured them all. Then Moses took up his staff, and behold, it returned to what it had been. When the sorcerers saw that, they said to Pharaoh: "We used to practise sorcery on the people, and when we overcame them the ropes and staffs would remain, and likewise if they overcame us. But this is the truth," so they prostrated and believed in the Lord of the worlds.

Know that there is disagreement in the reports. Some of them increased the number of the ropes and staffs, and some took a middle position, and Allah knows best the number of that. What the Qur'an indicates is that they were numerous, from the fact that they were gathered from every city, and because the affair reached such a magnitude for Pharaoh and his people that it is unlikely that he would withhold anything that could be done to gather the sorcerers.

* * *
As for His words: ﴿And they said, "By the might of Pharaoh, indeed we are the victors."﴾ The meaning is that they displayed what amounts to certainty that they would prevail, and all of that, when it became manifest, only strengthened the matter of Moses, peace be upon him.

When he says, ﴿Then Moses threw down his staff, and behold, it swallowed up what they were faking﴾, the meaning of ﴿what they were faking﴾ is what they turned away from its true reality through their magic and their guile, so that they made their ropes and staffs appear to be snakes moving about. He called those things "faking" as an intensification.

* * *

When he says, ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾, the meaning is that they fell down in prostration. This was because they were at the highest level of knowledge of magic, and therefore they knew the ultimate limits of magic. When they saw that and witnessed it going beyond the bounds of magic, they knew that it was not magic, and this was only by the blessing of their thorough mastery of the knowledge of magic. Then at that point they could not restrain themselves from throwing themselves to the ground in prostration, as if they had been seized and cast down. If it is asked, "Who is the agent of the throwing down, and what would it be if it were stated explicitly?" The answer is: it is God, Exalted, by what arose in their hearts of firm motives free from opposing considerations. But the better view is that we should not posit an agent, because "ulqiya" (was thrown down) means "fell down and collapsed."

As for his saying, ﴿The Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾, it is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to "the Lord of the worlds," because Pharaoh claimed lordship, so they wanted to dismiss him. The meaning of attributing [the Lord] to the two of them in that context is that He is the One who called Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them, to Himself.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 26, verse 49–51:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Said [Pharaoh]: "Have you believed in Him before I have given you permission? Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic. So you will come to know. I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you all."﴾ ﴿They said, "No harm. Indeed, we are to our Lord returning.﴾ ﴿Indeed, we aspire that our Lord will forgive us our sins because we were the first of the believers."﴾

Know that when they all believed, Pharaoh was not secure that the people would say: "These sorcerers, despite their number and their gathering, did not believe except out of knowledge of the correctness of the matter of Musa, peace be upon him, so they will follow the same path as them." So he confused the people and exaggerated in repelling [the people] from Musa, peace be upon him, in several respects:

The first of them: his saying: ﴿Have you believed in Him before I have given you permission?﴾ This implies that your hastening to believe in him indicates that you were inclined toward him, and this casts suspicion upon them, so perhaps they fell short in their magic in opposing him.

The second of them: his saying: ﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic.﴾ This is an explicit statement of what he had hinted at first, and his purpose from it is that they did this by collusion between them and Musa, peace be upon him, and fell short in magic so that the matter of Musa, peace be upon him, would appear. Otherwise, the sorcerers had the capacity to do what Musa, peace be upon him, did. This is a strong doubt for repelling those who accept his words.

The third of them: his saying: ﴿So you will come to know.﴾ This is an absolute threat and a severe intimidation.

The fourth of them: his saying: ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you all.﴾ This is the detailed threat. Cutting off the hand and the foot on opposite sides means cutting off the right hand and the left foot, and crucifixion is well known. There is no destruction stronger than that. The verse does not state whether he carried this out or did not. Then they responded to these words in two ways:

The first: their saying: ﴿No harm. Indeed, we are to our Lord returning.﴾ *Ḍurr* and *ḍayr* are one and the same. The meaning is not that if that occurred it would not harm; rather they meant by the comparison to what they knew of the abode of recompense.

Know that their saying: ﴿Indeed, we are to our Lord returning﴾ contains a noble subtlety, namely that they had reached such love of Allah, exalted is He, that they wanted nothing except to arrive at His presence, and that they did not believe out of desire for reward or fear of punishment, but their sole aim was the arrival at His good pleasure and immersion in the lights of His knowledge, and this is the highest rank of the *ṣiddīqīn* (the truthful ones).

The second response: their saying: ﴿Indeed, we aspire that our Lord will forgive us our sins﴾ is an indication from them to disbelief, sorcery and other things. The word "aspire" (ṭamʿ) in this place may signify certainty, like the saying of Ibrahim: ﴿And the One from whom I aspire that He will forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 82], and it may signify supposition, because a person does not know what will come after.

As for his saying: ﴿because we were the first of the believers﴾, the meaning is "because we were the first of the group who attended that stand," or the meaning may be specifically the sorcerers, or the subjects of Pharaoh, or the people of their time. It was also read as ﴿in case we were⁠﴾ with a kasra, and this is of the conditional form that is used by one who is just, and its parallel is the saying of one to someone who delays his wage: "If I have worked for you, then pay me my due."
