**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 26, verses 52–62:**

Allah's words: ﴿And We revealed to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants; you will certainly be pursued."﴾ ﴿So Pharaoh sent heralds into the cities.﴾ ﴿"Indeed, these are but a small band.﴾ ﴿And indeed, they have enraged us.﴾ ﴿And indeed, we are a vigilant host."﴾ ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿and treasures and a noble station.﴾ ﴿Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them.﴾ ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise.﴾ ﴿And when the two groups saw each other, the companions of Musa said: "Indeed, we are about to be overtaken."﴾ ﴿He said: "No! Indeed, my Lord is with me; He will guide me."﴾

The word ﴿أَسْرِ﴾ (asri, "travel by night") is read with a hamza of cutting (qat') and with a hamza of connection (wasl), and also as ﴿سِرْ﴾ (siri). When the matter of Musa, peace be upon him, became manifest through the sign that they had witnessed, Allah the Exalted commanded him to leave with the Children of Israel. This was because it was part of what was known of Allah's providence concerning Musa, and of rescuing him from the people and granting him their lands and wealth. Since that clear victory had taken place, he was not secure against Pharaoh doing something to the Children of Israel that would lead to their total destruction. Therefore Allah the Exalted commanded him to journey by night with the Children of Israel, who were the believers and were from the people of Musa. There is no doubt that the speech contains an ellipsis, namely that he did travel with them as Allah had commanded him. Then the people of Musa, peace be upon him, said to the people of Pharaoh: "We have a festival on this night." They then borrowed from them their jewelry and garments for this reason, and then they went out with those possessions at night toward the side of the sea. When Pharaoh heard of this, he sent heralds into the cities. Then he strengthened himself and his companions by describing the people of Musa with two of the attributes of blame, and describing his own people with an attribute of praise.

As for the description of the people of Musa, peace be upon him, with blame:

The first attribute is his saying: ﴿"Indeed, these are but a small band."﴾ The word ﴿شِرْذِمَةٌ﴾ (shirdhima, "small band") means a small group. From it comes their saying "shara'dhim" for a garment that has worn out and been torn into pieces. He named them with a noun indicating fewness, then described them as "few" with an adjective, then made the adjective plural, so that each group among them was "few." He chose the sound masculine plural (jam' al-salama, "sound plural"), which is used for paucity. It is also possible that by "fewness" he meant lowliness, not paucity of number. The meaning is: because of their fewness, he does not concern himself with them and does not expect them to overcome or prevail over him.

Then the exegetes differed about the number of that small band. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: they were six hundred thousand fighting men, with no youth under twenty years old and no elder over sixty, except for the servants. Pharaoh was making them seem few because of the multitude of those with him. This description may be used for a large number when compared with something even larger. It is narrated that Pharaoh went out on a dark bay stallion, and in his army, on horses of his color, were three hundred thousand.

The second attribute is his saying: ﴿"And indeed, they have enraged us."﴾ That is, they do deeds that enrage us and constrict our breasts. The exegetes differed about those deeds in several respects:

The first of them: what has preceded concerning the jewelry and other things.

The second: the departure of the Children of Israel from the servitude of Pharaoh and their independence by themselves.

The third: their opposition to them in religion and their rebellion against them.

The fourth: nothing other than that they did not take Pharaoh as a god.

As for what Pharaoh described his own people with, it is his saying: ﴿"And indeed, we are a vigilant host."﴾ In it there are three readings: ﴿حَذِرُونَ﴾ (hadhirun), ﴿حاذِرُونَ﴾ (hadhirun with an alif, ḥādhirūn), and ﴿حادِرُونَ﴾ (ḥādirūn), with the unpointed dal (dāl ghayr mu'jama).

Know that when the attribute is derived from the verb and is the active participle (ism al-fa'il) or the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), like "ḍārib" (one who strikes) and "maḍrūb" (one who is struck), it indicates occurrence and newness. When it is not so, being the attribute-like form (al-mushabbaha, "resembling form"), it indicates permanence. So whoever reads ﴿حَذِرُونَ﴾ goes to the meaning: we are a people whose custom is caution and the exercise of prudence. Whoever reads ﴿حاذِرُونَ﴾ seems to go to the meaning: we are a people who have known caution only in this our era. As for whoever reads ﴿حادِرُونَ﴾ with the unpointed dal, he seems to go to the negation of caution altogether, because ﴿الحادِرُ﴾ (al-ḥādir) is the one who girds up, so he meant: we are a people who are strong and fierce, or he meant: we are fully armed with weapons. The purpose of these excuses is that the people of the cities should not suppose that he was weakened before the people of Musa or was afraid of them.

As for his saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We expelled them﴾, the meaning is: We placed in their hearts the motive to leave, and the motive necessitated the act, so the act was necessarily ascribed to Allah the Exalted.

* * *

As for his saying: ﴿from gardens and springs﴾ ﴿and treasures﴾, Mujahid said: He called them treasures because they did not spend from them in obedience to Allah the Exalted. ﴿A noble station﴾ means good dwellings and splendid assemblies. The meaning is: We expelled them from their orchards in which were springs of water and treasures of gold and silver, and from the places in which they were living in luxury, in order to hand them over to the Children of Israel. As for his saying ﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾ (kadhalika, "thus"), it may have three grammatical possibilities: the accusative (naṣb), meaning "We expelled them in the manner of that expulsion which We have described"; the genitive (jarr), as an attribute of ﴿مَقَامٍ كَرِيمٍ﴾, meaning "a noble station like that station which they had"; and the nominative (raf'), as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "the matter is thus."

As for his saying: ﴿So they pursued them﴾, that is, they caught up with them. It is also read ﴿فَاتَّبَعُوهُمْ﴾ (fa-ittaba'uhum), and ﴿مُشْرِقِينَ﴾ (mushriqin, "at sunrise") means entering the time of sunrise, from "ashraqat al-shams" (the sun rose), when it rises.

As for his saying: ﴿And when the two groups saw each other﴾, that is, some of them saw others. The companions of Musa said: ﴿"Indeed, we are about to be overtaken."﴾ That is, we are about to be caught. [They said:] ﴿"We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 129]. They were slaughtering our sons, before you came to us and after you came to us. They would overtake us, meaning at that very moment, and kill us. It is also read ﴿فَلَمَّا تَرَاءَتِ الْفِئَتَانِ﴾ (when the two hosts saw each other) and ﴿إِنَّا لَمُدَّرَكُونَ﴾ (indeed we are about to be overtaken), with the dal doubled and the ra' kasra, from "idd-araka al-shay'" (the thing followed up on, one after another, until it perished). From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Rather, their knowledge has been exhausted concerning the Hereafter﴾ [An-Naml: 66]. Al-Hasan said: they were ignorant of the knowledge of the Hereafter. The meaning is: indeed we are being consecutively destroyed at their hands until none of us remains. At that point he said to them: ﴿"No!"﴾, and this is like a prohibition of what they supposed. Then he strengthened their souls with two matters:

The first: ﴿"Indeed, my Lord is with me."﴾ This indicates support and the assurance of help.

The second: his saying: ﴿"He will guide me."﴾ Guidance is the way of salvation and deliverance. When He guides him to the way of his salvation and the destruction of his enemies, He has reached the utmost in support.

He chose the sound masculine plural (jam' al-salama, "sound plural"), which is used for paucity. It is also possible that by "fewness" he meant lowliness, not paucity of number. The meaning is: because of their fewness, he does not concern himself with them and does not expect them to overcome or prevail over him.

The third: their opposition to them in religion and their rebellion against them.

The fourth: nothing other than that they did not take Pharaoh as a god.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 26, verses 63–68:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We inspired to Musa, "Strike the sea with your staff," and it parted, and each part was like a huge mountain.﴾ ﴿And We brought the others near there.﴾ ﴿And We saved Musa and those with him, all of them.﴾ ﴿Then We drowned the others.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed your Lord is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, related the words of Musa, peace be upon him, ﴿Indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾, He afterwards explained how He guided him, saved him, and destroyed his enemies through that arrangement, which combined the blessings of the religion and of this world. So He said: ﴿So We inspired to Musa, "Strike the sea with your staff," and it parted.﴾ There is no doubt that the meaning is "so he struck, and it parted," because this is understood from the speech, since it is not possible for it to part without a strike. Yet He commands him to strike, because otherwise it would be like futility; and because He made it one of his miracles that appeared through the staff; and because its parting by his striking is greater in blessing for him and stronger in establishing for them the knowledge that this occurred only on account of Musa, peace be upon him.

They differed concerning the sea. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that when Musa, peace be upon him, reached the sea with the Children of Israel, he commanded them to wade into the sea, but they refused except Yusha ibn Nun. He struck his mount and plunged into the sea until he crossed. Then he returned to them, but they refused to wade in. Musa said to the sea, "Part for me." It said, "I have not been commanded to do that, and the disobedient will not cross over me." Musa said, "O my Lord, the sea has refused to part." It was said to him, "Strike the sea with your staff," and he struck it, and it parted, and "each part was like a huge mountain," that is, like a great mountain, and within it there were twelve paths, one for each tribe. Each tribe said, "Our companions have been killed." At that, Musa, peace be upon him, supplicated his Lord, and He made them into windows like the shape of layers, so that some of them could see others on dry land. It is also related from Ata ibn al-Sa'ib that Jibril, peace be upon him, was between the Children of Israel and the family of Fir'awn, and he would say to the Children of Israel, "Let your last join your first," and he would confront the Copts and say, "Wait slowly, so that your last may catch up." And it is related that Musa, peace be upon him, said at that time: "O You who were before everything, who brings everything into being, and who remains after everything."

As for His saying: ﴿and each part was like a huge mountain﴾, the firq (part) is the portion separated from it. It was also recited as "kullu falq" (each cleft), and the meaning is one. The ṭawd is the lengthy mountain, that is, the one raised high into the sky. And it is miraculous in several respects:

First: that the separation of that water is a miracle.

Second: that the gathering of that water above each side of it, until it became like a mountain, is also among the miracles; for it was not impossible that the water which had been removed by that separation should be dispersed by Allah, the Exalted, until it became as though it had never been. So when it was gathered on both sides, it became a confirmation of this miracle.

Third: that if what is related in the report is established, that He, the Exalted, sent upon Fir'awn and his people winds and darkness which bewildered them, so that they were held back for the amount of time in which the crossing of the Children of Israel would be completed, then this is a third miracle.

Fourth: that Allah made in those watery walls openings through which some could look at others, and this is a fourth miracle.

Fifth: that Allah, the Exalted, kept those passages open until the family of Fir'awn drew near to them and hoped to escape from the sea as the people of Musa, peace be upon him, had escaped, and this is a fifth miracle.

[Page 122 — the text continues from the preceding page; see "صفحة ١٢١" above]

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We brought the others near there﴾, there are two discussions concerning it.

The first discussion: Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jurayj, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: "wa-azlafna" means "and We brought near," and "thamma" means "there," that is, where the sea split for the others, the people of Fir'awn. Concerning "thamma" there are three possibilities:

One: We brought them near to the Children of Israel.

Two: We brought some of them near to others and gathered them together so that not one of them would escape.

Three: We brought them forward to the sea. Some people have said: "wa-azlafna" means We held back Fir'awn and his people when they pursued Musa, peace be upon him, by darkening the world for them with a cloud that stood over them, so they stood bewildered. It was also recited as "wa-azlaqna" with a qaf, meaning "We made their feet slip," and the meaning is: We removed their might. It is also possible that Allah made their path in the sea different from that which He made dry for the Children of Israel, and He made them slip.

The second discussion: He, the Exalted, attributed that bringing near to Himself, although their gathering there in pursuit of Musa was disbelief. Al-Jubba'i answered this in two ways:

The first: The people of Fir'awn followed the Children of Israel, and the Children of Israel only did that by the command of Allah, the Exalted. Since their journey was by His arrangement, and these followed it, He attributed it to Himself figuratively. This is like one of us who is exhausted in pursuing his servant, and so he may say, "The servant has exhausted me, when such and such happened, he did it."

The second: It was said: ﴿And We brought the others near there﴾ means We brought them near to death, because at that time they had drawn near to their terms. And he recited:

*"Every day that has passed, or night that has elapsed, in which souls draw near to their appointed times."*

Al-Ka'bi answered this in two ways:

The first: When He, the Exalted, showed forbearance toward them and left the sea dry for them, and they hoped to cross it, the attribution became permissible, like a man whom his companion insults repeatedly and he shows forbearance toward him. But when he persists in his error and He shows him His power over him, He says to him: "I brought you to this and made you reach it through My forbearance." He does not mean by this that He intended what He did.

The second: It is possible that He brought them near, that is, gathered them so that He might drown them at that point, and so that they would not reach Musa and his people.

As for the answer to the first: whether what the Children of Israel did has any effect in drawing the motive of the people of Fir'awn to go after them or has no effect in it. If the first is the case, then the purpose is achieved, because the act of Allah, the Exalted, has an effect in bringing about the motive that necessitates that bringing near. If it has no effect at all, then the connection is severed, and so the attribution would not be fitting. As for when one of us exhausts himself pursuing his servant, it is only permissible for him to say, "That servant has exhausted me," because the servant's act becomes like the influence in bringing about that exhaustion; for whenever he does that act, it is apparent that it becomes known to the master, and whenever he knows it, his knowledge becomes a motive for him to that exhaustion and an influence upon it, and so the attribution is correct. In sum, according to us, the capable agent cannot act except by a motive; so the motive influences the capable agent becoming influential in that act, and therefore the attribution is fitting.

As for the answer to the second, which is that He brought them near in order to drown them: He, the Exalted, did not bring them near; rather they themselves drew near, and then the drowning occurred after that. So how is it permissible to attribute this bringing near to Allah, the Exalted? According to our position, it is permissible, because He, the Exalted, is the one who created the motive that results in that drawing near.

As for the answer to the third, which is that His forbearance toward them and His giving them respite led them to that: we say, does that forbearance have an effect in drawing this motive or not? The rest of the argument is as previously stated.

The answer to the fourth is exactly the answer to the second. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We saved Musa and those with him, all of them﴾ ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾: the meaning is that He, the Exalted, made the sea dry for Musa and his people until they came out of it, and He drowned Fir'awn and his people, because when their entry into the sea was complete, the water closed over them, and they drowned in that water.

[Page 122]

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾, the meaning is that what happened in the sea is a wondrous sign among the great signs, indicating His power, because none of mankind is able to do it; and indicating His wisdom, in that what occurred was a benefit in religion and in this world; and indicating the truthfulness of Musa, peace be upon him, in that it was a miracle for him; and as a lesson for those who take heed from it forever. Thus it becomes a warning against opposing the command of Allah, the Exalted, and the command of His Messenger. And there is in it a lesson for Muhammad (ﷺ), for He said after it: ﴿but most of them were not believers﴾. In that there is consolation for him, for he would grieve over the denial of his people despite the manifestation of miracles upon him. So Allah, the Exalted, alerted him through this mention that he has an example in Musa and others, for what appeared to Musa of these great miracles, which dazzle the minds, did not prevent most of them from denying him and disbelieving in him, despite their witnessing what they witnessed in the sea and elsewhere. Likewise, O Muhammad, do not be amazed at the denial of most of them toward you; be patient with their harm, for perhaps they will reform, and in this patience there is a confirmation of the proof against them.

\* \* \*

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed your Lord is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾, its connection to what precedes it is that the people, despite witnessing this dazzling sign, disbelieved. Then He, the Exalted, was Mighty and capable of destroying them; yet He did not destroy them, but bestowed upon them kinds of His mercy. This indicates the perfection of His mercy and the breadth of His generosity and bounty.

Two: We brought some of them near to others and gathered them together so that not one of them would escape.

Three: We brought them forward to the sea. It is also possible that Allah made their path in the sea different from that which He made dry for the Children of Israel, and He made them slip.

The first: The people of Fir'awn followed the Children of Israel, and the Children of Israel only did that by the command of Allah, the Exalted. Since their journey was by His arrangement, and these followed it, He attributed it to Himself figuratively. This is like one of us who is exhausted in pursuing his servant, and so he may say, "The servant has exhausted me, when such and such happened, he did it."

The second: It was said: ﴿And We brought the others near there﴾ means We brought them near to death, because at that time they had drawn near to their terms. And he recited:

He does not mean by this that He intended what He did.

The second: It is possible that He brought them near, that is, gathered them so that He might drown them at that point, and so that they would not reach Musa and his people.

As for the answer to the first: whether what the Children of Israel did has any effect in drawing the motive of the people of Fir'awn to go after them or has no effect in it. It is also related from Ata ibn al-Sa'ib that Jibril, peace be upon him, was between the Children of Israel and the family of Fir'awn, and he would say to the Children of Israel, "Let your last join your first," and he would confront the Copts and say, "Wait slowly, so that your last may catch up." And it is related that Musa, peace be upon him, said at that time: "O You who were before everything, who brings everything into being, and who remains after everything."

As for His saying: ﴿and each part was like a huge mountain﴾, the firq (part) is the portion separated from it. It was also recited as "kullu falq" (each cleft), and the meaning is one. The ṭawd is the lengthy mountain, that is, the one raised high into the sky. And it is miraculous in several respects:

First: that the separation of that water is a miracle.

Second: that the gathering of that water above each side of it, until it became like a mountain, is also among the miracles; for it was not impossible that the water which had been removed by that separation should be dispersed by Allah, the Exalted, until it became as though it had never been. So when it was gathered on both sides, it became a confirmation of this miracle.

Third: that if what is related in the report is established, that He, the Exalted, sent upon Fir'awn and his people winds and darkness which bewildered them, so that they were held back for the amount of time in which the crossing of the Children of Israel would be completed, then this is a third miracle.

Fourth: that Allah made in those watery walls openings through which some could look at others, and this is a fourth miracle.

Fifth: that Allah, the Exalted, kept those passages open until the family of Fir'awn drew near to them and hoped to escape from the sea as the people of Musa, peace be upon him, had escaped, and this is a fifth miracle.

[Page 122 — the text continues from the preceding page; see "صفحة ١٢١" above]

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We brought the others near there﴾, there are two discussions concerning it.

The first discussion: Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jurayj, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: "wa-azlafna" means "and We brought near," and "thamma" means "there," that is, where the sea split for the others, the people of Fir'awn. Concerning "thamma" there are three possibilities:

One: We brought them near to the Children of Israel.

Two: We brought some of them near to others and gathered them together so that not one of them would escape.

Three: We brought them forward to the sea. Some people have said: "wa-azlafna" means We held back Fir'awn and his people when they pursued Musa, peace be upon him, by darkening the world for them with a cloud that stood over them, so they stood bewildered. It was also recited as "wa-azlaqna" with a qaf, meaning "We made their feet slip," and the meaning is: We removed their might. It is also possible that Allah made their path in the sea different from that which He made dry for the Children of Israel, and He made them slip.

The second discussion: He, the Exalted, attributed that bringing near to Himself, although their gathering there in pursuit of Musa was disbelief. Al-Jubba'i answered this in two ways:

The first: The people of Fir'awn followed the Children of Israel, and the Children of Israel only did that by the command of Allah, the Exalted. Since their journey was by His arrangement, and these followed it, He attributed it to Himself figuratively. This is like one of us who is exhausted in pursuing his servant, and so he may say, "The servant has exhausted me, when such and such happened, he did it."

The second: It was said: ﴿And We brought the others near there﴾ means We brought them near to death, because at that time they had drawn near to their terms. And he recited:

*"Every day that has passed, or night that has elapsed, in which souls draw near to their appointed times."*

Al-Ka'bi answered this in two ways:

The first: When He, the Exalted, showed forbearance toward them and left the sea dry for them, and they hoped to cross it, the attribution became permissible, like a man whom his companion insults repeatedly and he shows forbearance toward him. But when he persists in his error and He shows him His power over him, He says to him: "I brought you to this and made you reach it through My forbearance." He does not mean by this that He intended what He did.

The second: It is possible that He brought them near, that is, gathered them so that He might drown them at that point, and so that they would not reach Musa and his people.

As for the answer to the first: whether what the Children of Israel did has any effect in drawing the motive of the people of Fir'awn to go after them or has no effect in it. If the first is the case, then the purpose is achieved, because the act of Allah, the Exalted, has an effect in bringing about the motive that necessitates that bringing near. If it has no effect at all, then the connection is severed, and so the attribution would not be fitting. As for when one of us exhausts himself pursuing his servant, it is only permissible for him to say, "That servant has exhausted me," because the servant's act becomes like the influence in bringing about that exhaustion; for whenever he does that act, it is apparent that it becomes known to the master, and whenever he knows it, his knowledge becomes a motive for him to that exhaustion and an influence upon it, and so the attribution is correct. In sum, according to us, the capable agent cannot act except by a motive; so the motive influences the capable agent becoming influential in that act, and therefore the attribution is fitting.

As for the answer to the second, which is that He brought them near in order to drown them: He, the Exalted, did not bring them near; rather they themselves drew near, and then the drowning occurred after that. So how is it permissible to attribute this bringing near to Allah, the Exalted? According to our position, it is permissible, because He, the Exalted, is the one who created the motive that results in that drawing near.

As for the answer to the third, which is that His forbearance toward them and His giving them respite led them to that: we say, does that forbearance have an effect in drawing this motive or not? The rest of the argument is as previously stated.

The answer to the fourth is exactly the answer to the second. And Allah knows best.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We saved Musa and those with him, all of them﴾ ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾: the meaning is that He, the Exalted, made the sea dry for Musa and his people until they came out of it, and He drowned Fir'awn and his people, because when their entry into the sea was complete, the water closed over them, and they drowned in that water.

[Page 122]

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾, the meaning is that what happened in the sea is a wondrous sign among the great signs, indicating His power, because none of mankind is able to do it; and indicating His wisdom, in that what occurred was a benefit in religion and in this world; and indicating the truthfulness of Musa, peace be upon him, in that it was a miracle for him; and as a lesson for those who take heed from it forever. Thus it becomes a warning against opposing the command of Allah, the Exalted, and the command of His Messenger. And there is in it a lesson for Muhammad (ﷺ), for He said after it: ﴿but most of them were not believers﴾. In that there is consolation for him, for he would grieve over the denial of his people despite the manifestation of miracles upon him. So Allah, the Exalted, alerted him through this mention that he has an example in Musa and others, for what appeared to Musa of these great miracles, which dazzle the minds, did not prevent most of them from denying him and disbelieving in him, despite their witnessing what they witnessed in the sea and elsewhere. Likewise, O Muhammad, do not be amazed at the denial of most of them toward you; be patient with their harm, for perhaps they will reform, and in this patience there is a confirmation of the proof against them.

\* \* \*

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed your Lord is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾, its connection to what precedes it is that the people, despite witnessing this dazzling sign, disbelieved. Then He, the Exalted, was Mighty and capable of destroying them; yet He did not destroy them, but bestowed upon them kinds of His mercy. This indicates the perfection of His mercy and the breadth of His generosity and bounty.

**The second story: the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him)**

﴿And recite to them the news of Ibrahim.﴾ ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do they hear you when you call?"﴾ ﴿Or do they benefit you or harm you?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Rather, we found our fathers doing thus."﴾ ﴿He said, "Have you considered what you have been worshipping,﴾ ﴿you and your fathers before you?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds."﴾

The Exalted said: ﴿And recite to them the news of Ibrahim.﴾ ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?"﴾ ﴿They said, "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do they hear you when you call?"﴾ ﴿Or do they benefit you or harm you?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Rather, we found our fathers doing thus."﴾ ﴿He said, "Have you considered what you have been worshipping,﴾ ﴿you and your fathers before you?"﴾ ﴿Indeed, they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds."﴾

Know that at the beginning of the surah, the Exalted mentioned the intensity of the grief of Muhammad (ﷺ) because of the disbelief of his people. Then He mentioned the story of Musa (peace be upon him), so that Muhammad would know that a similar trial had befallen Musa. Then after it He mentioned the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), so that Muhammad would also know that the grief of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) for this same reason was greater than his own grief. This is because among the great trials of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was that he saw his father and his people in the Fire, and he could not rescue them except by means of supplication and admonition. So he said to them, ﴿What do you worship?﴾ Ibrahim (peace be upon him) knew that they were idol-worshippers, but he asked them in order to show them that what they worshipped did not deserve worship at all. It is like when you say to a slave-trader, "What is your wealth?" while you know that his wealth is slaves, and then you say, "Slaves are a beauty, not a wealth."

They answered Ibrahim (peace be upon him) with their words: ﴿We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them.﴾ *Al-ʿukūf* means staying constantly upon something. They said *fa-naẓall* (and we remain) because they used to worship them by day and not by night. Know that for the answer it would have been sufficient for them to say, "We worship idols," but they added to the answer an extra part, which is their saying, ﴿and we remain devoted to them.﴾ They mentioned this addition only to display what was in their souls of pride and boastfulness in worshipping idols. So Ibrahim (peace be upon him), alerting them to the corruption of their position, said: ﴿Do they hear you when you call?﴾ ﴿Or do they benefit you or harm you?﴾

The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: In *yasmaʿūnakum* there must be an assumed omission of a word that is attached (*al-muḍāf*), meaning: "Do they hear your supplication?" Qatada recited *hal yusmiʿūnakum* (do they make you hear), meaning: "Do they make you hear the answer to your supplication? And are they able to do that?"

The explanation of this argument that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) presented is that, generally, the condition of one who worships another is that he turns to him with his request, so that he (the one worshipped) may know his need when he hears his supplication, and then respond to him by granting some benefit or repelling some harm. So he said to them: If the one you worship does not hear your supplication until he knows your intention, and even if he knew it, it would not be right for him to grant benefit or repel harm, then how do you consider it permissible to worship what has this description? At this decisive argument, his father and his people did not find anything with which to repel this argument, so they turned to saying: ﴿We found our fathers doing thus.﴾ This is one of the strongest proofs of the corruption of *taqlid* (blind imitation) and of the obligation to hold fast to *istidlal* (reasoned inference). For if we reversed the matter, praising *taqlid* and blaming *istidlal*, that would be a praise of the way of the disbelievers, which Allah the Exalted condemned, and a condemnation of the way of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), which Allah the Exalted praised. So Ibrahim (peace be upon him) answered them with his saying: ﴿He said, "Have you considered what you have been worshipping,﴾ ﴿you and your fathers before you?"﴾ By this he meant that falsehood does not change by being ancient or recent, nor by its adherents being many or few.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds,﴾ there are questions concerning it:

**The first question:** How can an idol be an enemy when it is inanimate? Its answer is in two respects:

The first: The Exalted said in the surah of Maryam, concerning the description of the idols: ﴿No! They will deny their worship of them and will be opposed to them﴾ [Maryam: 82]. It was said in its interpretation that Allah will revive the idols that they worshipped, so that they will reproach them and disown them. On this view, the idols will become enemies to these disbelievers in the Hereafter. Thus Ibrahim (peace be upon him) used the word "enemy" for them according to this interpretation.

The second: When the disbelievers worshipped them, exalted them, and hoped in them for obtaining benefits and warding off harms, they came to occupy the position of living, rational beings in the belief of the disbelievers. Then they became causes of a person's deprivation of happiness and his arrival at wretchedness. Since these idols were placed in the position of living beings and functioned as the one who repels benefit and brings harm, they were, as a matter of course, treated as enemies. Therefore Ibrahim (peace be upon him) applied the word "enemy" to them.

The third: What is meant by His saying, ﴿Indeed, they are enemies to me,﴾ is the enmity of those who worship them. If it is said: Why did he not say, "Indeed, those who worship idols are enemies to me," so that the statement would be literal? Its answer: Because what was previously mentioned was what they worshipped, not the worshippers.

**The second question:** Why did he say, ﴿Indeed, they are enemies to me,﴾ and not say, "Indeed, they are enemies to you"? Its answer: He (peace be upon him) presented the matter as concerning himself, in the sense of: "I reflected upon my own affair and saw that my worship of them was worship of an enemy, so I avoided it." He showed them that it was advice that he gave to himself. So when they reflect, they will say: "Ibrahim gave us no advice except what he gave to himself," and that will be more likely to make it accepted.

**The third question:** Why did he not say, "Indeed, they are my enemies" (in the plural)? Its answer: *al-ʿaduww* (enemy) and *al-ṣadīq* (friend) may be used with the meaning of the singular and the plural. A poet said:

*"And a people over me, possessed of harshness, I see them as enemies, though they were friends."*

From this is His saying: ﴿and they are enemies to you﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ? / other verses], and the verification of this matter has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds.﴾

**The fourth question:** What is this exception? Its answer: It is a disjunctive exception (*istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ*), as if he had said: "But the Lord of the worlds."

[p. 123]

So he said to them, ﴿What do you worship?﴾ Ibrahim (peace be upon him) knew that they were idol-worshippers, but he asked them in order to show them that what they worshipped did not deserve worship at all. It is like when you say to a slave-trader, "What is your wealth?" while you know that his wealth is slaves, and then you say, "Slaves are a beauty, not a wealth."

They answered Ibrahim (peace be upon him) with their words: ﴿We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them.﴾ *Al-ʿukūf* means staying constantly upon something. They said *fa-naẓall* (and we remain) because they used to worship them by day and not by night. Know that for the answer it would have been sufficient for them to say, "We worship idols," but they added to the answer an extra part, which is their saying, ﴿and we remain devoted to them.﴾ They mentioned this addition only to display what was in their souls of pride and boastfulness in worshipping idols. So Ibrahim (peace be upon him), alerting them to the corruption of their position, said: ﴿Do they hear you when you call?﴾ ﴿Or do they benefit you or harm you?﴾

The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: In *yasmaʿūnakum* there must be an assumed omission of a word that is attached (*al-muḍāf*), meaning: "Do they hear your supplication?" Qatada recited *hal yusmiʿūnakum* (do they make you hear), meaning: "Do they make you hear the answer to your supplication? And are they able to do that?"

The explanation of this argument that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) presented is that, generally, the condition of one who worships another is that he turns to him with his request, so that he (the one worshipped) may know his need when he hears his supplication, and then respond to him by granting some benefit or repelling some harm. So he said to them: If the one you worship does not hear your supplication until he knows your intention, and even if he knew it, it would not be right for him to grant benefit or repel harm, then how do you consider it permissible to worship what has this description? At this decisive argument, his father and his people did not find anything with which to repel this argument, so they turned to saying: ﴿We found our fathers doing thus.﴾ This is one of the strongest proofs of the corruption of *taqlid* (blind imitation) and of the obligation to hold fast to *istidlal* (reasoned inference). For if we reversed the matter, praising *taqlid* and blaming *istidlal*, that would be a praise of the way of the disbelievers, which Allah the Exalted condemned, and a condemnation of the way of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), which Allah the Exalted praised. So Ibrahim (peace be upon him) answered them with his saying: ﴿He said, "Have you considered what you have been worshipping,﴾ ﴿you and your fathers before you?"﴾ By this he meant that falsehood does not change by being ancient or recent, nor by its adherents being many or few.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, they are enemies to me, except the Lord of the worlds,﴾ there are questions concerning it:

**The first question:** How can an idol be an enemy when it is inanimate? Its answer is in two respects:

The first: The Exalted said in the surah of Maryam, concerning the description of the idols: ﴿No! They will deny their worship of them and will be opposed to them﴾ [Maryam: 82]. It was said in its interpretation that Allah will revive the idols that they worshipped, so that they will reproach them and disown them. On this view, the idols will become enemies to these disbelievers in the Hereafter. Thus Ibrahim (peace be upon him) used the word "enemy" for them according to this interpretation.

The second: When the disbelievers worshipped them, exalted them, and hoped in them for obtaining benefits and warding off harms, they came to occupy the position of living, rational beings in the belief of the disbelievers. Then they became causes of a person's deprivation of happiness and his arrival at wretchedness. Since these idols were placed in the position of living beings and functioned as the one who repels benefit and brings harm, they were, as a matter of course, treated as enemies. Therefore Ibrahim (peace be upon him) applied the word "enemy" to them.

The third: What is meant by His saying, ﴿Indeed, they are enemies to me,﴾ is the enmity of those who worship them. If it is said: Why did he not say, "Indeed, those who worship idols are enemies to me," so that the statement would be literal? Its answer: Because what was previously mentioned was what they worshipped, not the worshippers.

**The second question:** Why did he say, ﴿Indeed, they are enemies to me,﴾ and not say, "Indeed, they are enemies to you"? Its answer: He (peace be upon him) presented the matter as concerning himself, in the sense of: "I reflected upon my own affair and saw that my worship of them was worship of an enemy, so I avoided it." He showed them that it was advice that he gave to himself. So when they reflect, they will say: "Ibrahim gave us no advice except what he gave to himself," and that will be more likely to make it accepted.

**The third question:** Why did he not say, "Indeed, they are my enemies" (in the plural)? Its answer: *al-ʿaduww* (enemy) and *al-ṣadīq* (friend) may be used with the meaning of the singular and the plural. A poet said:

*"And a people over me, possessed of harshness, I see them as enemies, though they were friends."*

From this is His saying: ﴿and they are enemies to you﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ? / other verses], and the verification of this matter has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds.﴾

**The fourth question:** What is this exception? Its answer: It is a disjunctive exception (*istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ*), as if he had said: "But the Lord of the worlds."

Allah, the Exalted, when He related that he (Abraham) made an exception for the Lord of the worlds, also related the attributes by which He is described as deserving worship, and then related what he asked of Him. As for the attributes, there are four:

The first of them is His saying: ﴿Who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾.

Know that He, glorified is He, praised Himself with these two matters in His saying: ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ and ﴿And who determined and then guided﴾ [al-A'la: 2, 3]. Know that through creation and guidance all benefits are obtained for everyone who is able to benefit. Let us speak about the human being. We say: he is a created being. Some have said he belongs to the world of creation and corporeal things (al-khalq wa al-jismaniyyat), and others have said he belongs to the world of command (al-amr) and spiritual things (al-ruhaniyyat). The composition of the body, which belongs to the world of creation, precedes the bestowing of the heart, which belongs to the world of command, as He, glorified is He, informed in His saying: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit﴾ [al-Hijr: 29]. Thus "proportioning" refers to the balancing of temperament (ta'dil al-mizaj) and the composition of the mixed elements (tarkib al-amshaj), and "breathing of the spirit" refers to the divine, luminous subtle essence (al-latifa al-rabbaniyya al-nuraniyya) which belongs to the world of command. Also, He said: ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12], and when He completed the stages of the changes of bodies, He said: ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14]. That refers to the spirit, which belongs to the world of the angels. There is no doubt that guidance is only attained through the spirit. Thus it has become clear from these verses that creation precedes guidance.

As for its verification according to the real investigations: the human body is only generated when the seed (al-maniyy) mixes with the menstrual blood (dam al-tamth), and these two are only generated from foods, which are produced from the composition and interaction of the four elements. When the seed mixes with the blood, what is in them of the hot, the cold, the moist and the dry continues to interact, and what is in each one of them of powers breaks the violence of the quality of the other. Then from their interaction there results an intermediate quality, which is warm in relation to the cold and cool in relation to the hot. The same is said about the moist and the dry. Then the readiness is achieved for receiving powers that regulate that composite. Some of these are vegetative powers (quwan nabatiyya), namely those which draw in nourishment, then retain it, then digest it, then expel the harmful residue, then restore those parts in place of what has dissolved from them, then increase the substance of the organs in length and breadth. Then from those materials there remains a residue from which something similar can be generated. Some of them are animal powers (quwan hayawaniyya): some are perceptive, like the five senses, imagination, retention and recollection; and some are active, either commanding, like desire and anger, or commanded, like the powers embedded in the muscles. Some of them are human powers (quwan insaniyya), which are either perceptive or operative. The perceptive powers are the powers capable of perceiving the realities of things, spiritual and corporeal, higher and lower. Then, if you examine each one of the composites of this corporeal world and its simple elements, you will find for each of them things that suit it and complete its condition, and things that repel it and corrupt its condition, and you will find in them powers that attract what suits and repel what opposes. Thus it has become clear that the wellbeing of the condition of these things is not complete except through creation and guidance. As for creation, it is by making it existent after it was non-existent. As for guidance, it is by those powers that attract benefits and repel harms. Therefore it is established that His saying ﴿who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ is a comprehensive phrase containing all benefits in this world and the religion.

Then here there is a subtle point: He said ﴿created me﴾, mentioning it in the past tense, and He said ﴿guides me﴾, mentioning it in the future tense. The reason for that is that the creation of the essence does not renew itself in this world; rather, once it has occurred, it remains until the known term. As for His guidance, it is something that recurs at every moment and time, whether that guidance is in worldly benefits, which is by the senses' discrimination between benefits and harms, or in religious benefits, which is by the intellect judging between truth and falsehood, and good and evil. Thus He made clear that He is the One who created him with all that his creation was completed with in the past at once, and that He guides him to the interests of religion and this world with various kinds of guidance in every moment and glance.

The second: His saying ﴿And it is He who feeds me and gives me drink﴾. It includes everything connected with the benefits of sustenance. That is because, when He, glorified is He, creates food for him and grants him possession of it, if he did not have with it what enables him to eat it and nourish himself with it, by way of appetite, strength and discernment, this blessing would not be complete. He mentioned food and drink and, by mentioning them, drew attention to what is beyond them.

The third: His saying ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾. Here there is a question: why did he say ﴿I am ill﴾ and not ﴿He made me ill﴾? The answer has several aspects.

The first: many causes of illness occur through a person's negligence in his food, drink and other matters. For this reason the wise said: if most of the dead were asked, "What is the cause of your deaths?", they would say, "Overeating."

The second: illness only occurs through the dominance of some humours over others, and that dominance only happens because of the natural antagonism between them. Health, however, is achieved when the humours remain in their balance, and their remaining in balance only happens through a compelling cause that forces them to come together. And their return to health only happens through a compelling cause that forces them to return to togetherness and balance after they had, by their nature, been longing for separation and conflict. For this reason, He, glorified and exalted is He, attributed healing to Himself and did not attribute illness to Himself.

The third: healing is beloved and is among the foundations of blessings, and the intent of Abraham (peace be upon him) was to enumerate blessings. Since illness is not among the blessings, he did not attribute it to Him, the Exalted. If you object to this with death, the answer is that death is not a harm, because the condition for something to be harmful is that one perceives it, and at the moment of death no perception occurs. The harm lies in its preliminaries, and that is the very same as illness. Furthermore, you have come to know that when souls are perfected in knowledge and morals, their remaining in these bodies is itself harm, and their release from them is itself happiness, unlike illness.

The fourth: His saying ﴿And who causes me to die, then gives me life﴾. What is meant by it is death in this world and deliverance from its calamities and punishments, and what is meant by life is recompense.

The fifth: His saying ﴿And who I hope will forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense﴾. It refers to what every intelligent person seeks: deliverance from punishment and success with reward.

Know that Abraham (peace be upon him) gathered in these words all the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, from the beginning of creation to the end of eternity in the Hereafter.

Here there are questions:

The first question: Why did he say ﴿who I hope﴾, when hope (al-tama') is an expression for supposition and expectation, while he (peace be upon him) was certain of that? The answer: this statement is only consistent with our school, where we say that nothing is obligatory upon Allah for anyone, that everything is permissible from Him, and that no one has any objection to His action. Al-Jubba'i (Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i) answered it in two ways:

The first: His saying ﴿who I hope will forgive me my sin﴾ means all the believers, because they are the ones who hope and do not claim certainty.

The second: what is meant by hope is certainty, and this is related from al-Hasan (al-Basri). The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) answered: he mentioned it in this way to teach his community how to supplicate.

Know that these answers are weak.

As for the first: Allah, the Exalted, related from him praise first and supplication second, and from the beginning of the praise to the end of the supplication is the speech of Abraham (peace be upon him). So to make the one phrase ﴿who I hope will forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense﴾ the speech of someone else destroys and corrupts the arrangement of the speech.

As for the second, that hope means certainty, this goes against the language.

As for the third, that the purpose is to teach the community, this is also false, because its conclusion returns to the claim that he lied about himself for the purpose of teaching the community, and that is definitively false.

The second question: Why did he attribute sin to himself, when the prophets are definitively free from sins? In its answer there are three aspects:

The first: it is to be understood as a lie of Abraham (peace be upon him) in His saying: ﴿Rather, this was done by the largest of them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 63], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], and his saying to Sarah: "She is my sister." This is weak, because attributing lying to him is not permissible.

The second: he mentioned it as a form of humility and self-abasement. This is weak, because if he was truthful in this humility, the problem remains; and if he was lying, then the answer returns to attributing disobedience to him in order to exonerate him from disobedience.

The third, which is the correct answer: that it be understood as abandoning what is better (tark al-awla). This is sometimes called "error," because whoever owns a jewel and is able to sell it for a million dinars, if he sells it for one dinar, it is said that he erred. And abandoning what is better is permissible for the prophets.

The third question: Why did he tie the forgiveness of sin to the Day of Recompense, when it is forgiven in this world? The answer: because its effect appears on the Day of Recompense, and now it is hidden and not known.

The fourth question: What is the benefit of "to me" (li) in His saying ﴿that He may forgive me my sin﴾? The answer has several aspects:

The first: when a father pardons his son, a master his slave, or a husband his wife, this, in most cases, is only done to seek reward and flee punishment, or to seek good praise and commendation, or to relieve the pain arising from natural tenderness. And if that is the case, the purpose of that pardon is not to care for the one pardoned, but to care for oneself, either to attain what is fitting or to ward off what is not fitting. As for the Divine, glorified is He, He is perfect in His essence, so it is impossible for attributes of perfection to newly arise in Him, or for a deficiency that existed to be removed from Him. And if that is so, His pardon is nothing but care for the one pardoned. So His saying ﴿And the One I hope will forgive me﴾ means: He is the One who, when He forgives, His forgiveness is for me and for my sake, not for a matter that returns to Him at all.

The second: it is as if he said: You created me, not for my sake, for when You created me I was not existent, and when I was not existent it is impossible for anything to be achieved for my sake. Yet despite this, You created me. As for if You pardon me, that pardon would be for my sake. So since You created me first, though I was in need of that creation, then it is more fitting that You forgive me and pardon me at the time I am in the greatest need of pardon and forgiveness.

The third: Abraham (peace be upon him), because of the intensity of his immersion in the sea of knowledge, was intensely averse to turning toward intermediaries. For this reason, when Gabriel (peace be upon him) said to him: "Do you have a need?" he said: "As for you, no." So here he said: ﴿I hope that He will forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense﴾, meaning: merely because of my servitude to You and my need of You, You forgive my sin, not that You forgive it for me through the intercession of an intercessor.

Know that He, glorified is He, praised Himself with these two matters in His saying: ﴿Who created and proportioned﴾ and ﴿And who determined and then guided﴾ [al-A'la: 2, 3]. Know that through creation and guidance all benefits are obtained for everyone who is able to benefit. Let us speak about the human being. We say: he is a created being. Some have said he belongs to the world of creation and corporeal things (al-khalq wa al-jismaniyyat), and others have said he belongs to the world of command (al-amr) and spiritual things (al-ruhaniyyat). The composition of the body, which belongs to the world of creation, precedes the bestowing of the heart, which belongs to the world of command, as He, glorified is He, informed in His saying: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit﴾ [al-Hijr: 29]. Thus "proportioning" refers to the balancing of temperament (ta'dil al-mizaj) and the composition of the mixed elements (tarkib al-amshaj), and "breathing of the spirit" refers to the divine, luminous subtle essence (al-latifa al-rabbaniyya al-nuraniyya) which belongs to the world of command. Also, He said: ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12], and when He completed the stages of the changes of bodies, He said: ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14]. That refers to the spirit, which belongs to the world of the angels. There is no doubt that guidance is only attained through the spirit. Thus it has become clear from these verses that creation precedes guidance.

As for its verification according to the real investigations: the human body is only generated when the seed (al-maniyy) mixes with the menstrual blood (dam al-tamth), and these two are only generated from foods, which are produced from the composition and interaction of the four elements. When the seed mixes with the blood, what is in them of the hot, the cold, the moist and the dry continues to interact, and what is in each one of them of powers breaks the violence of the quality of the other. Then from their interaction there results an intermediate quality, which is warm in relation to the cold and cool in relation to the hot. The same is said about the moist and the dry. Then the readiness is achieved for receiving powers that regulate that composite. Some of these are vegetative powers (quwan nabatiyya), namely those which draw in nourishment, then retain it, then digest it, then expel the harmful residue, then restore those parts in place of what has dissolved from them, then increase the substance of the organs in length and breadth. Then from those materials there remains a residue from which something similar can be generated. Some of them are animal powers (quwan hayawaniyya): some are perceptive, like the five senses, imagination, retention and recollection; and some are active, either commanding, like desire and anger, or commanded, like the powers embedded in the muscles. Some of them are human powers (quwan insaniyya), which are either perceptive or operative. The perceptive powers are the powers capable of perceiving the realities of things, spiritual and corporeal, higher and lower. Then, if you examine each one of the composites of this corporeal world and its simple elements, you will find for each of them things that suit it and complete its condition, and things that repel it and corrupt its condition, and you will find in them powers that attract what suits and repel what opposes. Thus it has become clear that the wellbeing of the condition of these things is not complete except through creation and guidance. As for creation, it is by making it existent after it was non-existent. As for guidance, it is by those powers that attract benefits and repel harms. Therefore it is established that His saying ﴿who created me, and it is He who guides me﴾ is a comprehensive phrase containing all benefits in this world and the religion.

Then here there is a subtle point: He said ﴿created me﴾, mentioning it in the past tense, and He said ﴿guides me﴾, mentioning it in the future tense. The reason for that is that the creation of the essence does not renew itself in this world; rather, once it has occurred, it remains until the known term. As for His guidance, it is something that recurs at every moment and time, whether that guidance is in worldly benefits, which is by the senses' discrimination between benefits and harms, or in religious benefits, which is by the intellect judging between truth and falsehood, and good and evil. Thus He made clear that He is the One who created him with all that his creation was completed with in the past at once, and that He guides him to the interests of religion and this world with various kinds of guidance in every moment and glance.

The second: His saying ﴿And it is He who feeds me and gives me drink﴾. It includes everything connected with the benefits of sustenance. That is because, when He, glorified is He, creates food for him and grants him possession of it, if he did not have with it what enables him to eat it and nourish himself with it, by way of appetite, strength and discernment, this blessing would not be complete. He mentioned food and drink and, by mentioning them, drew attention to what is beyond them.

The third: His saying ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾. Here there is a question: why did he say ﴿I am ill﴾ and not ﴿He made me ill﴾? The answer has several aspects.

The first: many causes of illness occur through a person's negligence in his food, drink and other matters. For this reason the wise said: if most of the dead were asked, "What is the cause of your deaths?", they would say, "Overeating."

The second: illness only occurs through the dominance of some humours over others, and that dominance only happens because of the natural antagonism between them. Health, however, is achieved when the humours remain in their balance, and their remaining in balance only happens through a compelling cause that forces them to come together. And their return to health only happens through a compelling cause that forces them to return to togetherness and balance after they had, by their nature, been longing for separation and conflict. For this reason, He, glorified and exalted is He, attributed healing to Himself and did not attribute illness to Himself.

The third: healing is beloved and is among the foundations of blessings, and the intent of Abraham (peace be upon him) was to enumerate blessings. Since illness is not among the blessings, he did not attribute it to Him, the Exalted. If you object to this with death, the answer is that death is not a harm, because the condition for something to be harmful is that one perceives it, and at the moment of death no perception occurs. The harm lies in its preliminaries, and that is the very same as illness. Furthermore, you have come to know that when souls are perfected in knowledge and morals, their remaining in these bodies is itself harm, and their release from them is itself happiness, unlike illness.

The fourth: His saying ﴿And who causes me to die, then gives me life﴾. What is meant by it is death in this world and deliverance from its calamities and punishments, and what is meant by life is recompense.

The fifth: His saying ﴿And who I hope will forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense﴾. It refers to what every intelligent person seeks: deliverance from punishment and success with reward.

Know that Abraham (peace be upon him) gathered in these words all the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, from the beginning of creation to the end of eternity in the Hereafter.

* * *

Here there are questions:

The first question: Why did he say ﴿who I hope﴾, when hope (al-tama') is an expression for supposition and expectation, while he (peace be upon him) was certain of that? The answer: this statement is only consistent with our school, where we say that nothing is obligatory upon Allah for anyone, that everything is permissible from Him, and that no one has any objection to His action. Al-Jubba'i (Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i) answered it in two ways:

The first: His saying ﴿who I hope will forgive me my sin﴾ means all the believers, because they are the ones who hope and do not claim certainty.

The second: what is meant by hope is certainty, and this is related from al-Hasan (al-Basri). The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) answered: he mentioned it in this way to teach his community how to supplicate.

Know that these answers are weak.

As for the first: Allah, the Exalted, related from him praise first and supplication second, and from the beginning of the praise to the end of the supplication is the speech of Abraham (peace be upon him). So to make the one phrase ﴿who I hope will forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense﴾ the speech of someone else destroys and corrupts the arrangement of the speech.

As for the second, that hope means certainty, this goes against the language.

As for the third, that the purpose is to teach the community, this is also false, because its conclusion returns to the claim that he lied about himself for the purpose of teaching the community, and that is definitively false.

The second question: Why did he attribute sin to himself, when the prophets are definitively free from sins? In its answer there are three aspects:

The first: it is to be understood as a lie of Abraham (peace be upon him) in His saying: ﴿Rather, this was done by the largest of them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 63], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], and his saying to Sarah: "She is my sister." This is weak, because attributing lying to him is not permissible.

The second: he mentioned it as a form of humility and self-abasement. This is weak, because if he was truthful in this humility, the problem remains; and if he was lying, then the answer returns to attributing disobedience to him in order to exonerate him from disobedience.

The third, which is the correct answer: that it be understood as abandoning what is better (tark al-awla). This is sometimes called "error," because whoever owns a jewel and is able to sell it for a million dinars, if he sells it for one dinar, it is said that he erred. And abandoning what is better is permissible for the prophets.

The third question: Why did he tie the forgiveness of sin to the Day of Recompense, when it is forgiven in this world? The answer: because its effect appears on the Day of Recompense, and now it is hidden and not known.

The fourth question: What is the benefit of "to me" (li) in His saying ﴿that He may forgive me my sin﴾? The answer has several aspects:

The first: when a father pardons his son, a master his slave, or a husband his wife, this, in most cases, is only done to seek reward and flee punishment, or to seek good praise and commendation, or to relieve the pain arising from natural tenderness. And if that is the case, the purpose of that pardon is not to care for the one pardoned, but to care for oneself, either to attain what is fitting or to ward off what is not fitting. As for the Divine, glorified is He, He is perfect in His essence, so it is impossible for attributes of perfection to newly arise in Him, or for a deficiency that existed to be removed from Him. And if that is so, His pardon is nothing but care for the one pardoned. So His saying ﴿And the One I hope will forgive me﴾ means: He is the One who, when He forgives, His forgiveness is for me and for my sake, not for a matter that returns to Him at all.

The second: it is as if he said: You created me, not for my sake, for when You created me I was not existent, and when I was not existent it is impossible for anything to be achieved for my sake. Yet despite this, You created me. As for if You pardon me, that pardon would be for my sake. So since You created me first, though I was in need of that creation, then it is more fitting that You forgive me and pardon me at the time I am in the greatest need of pardon and forgiveness.

The third: Abraham (peace be upon him), because of the intensity of his immersion in the sea of knowledge, was intensely averse to turning toward intermediaries. For this reason, when Gabriel (peace be upon him) said to him: "Do you have a need?" he said: "As for you, no." So here he said: ﴿I hope that He will forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense﴾, meaning: merely because of my servitude to You and my need of You, You forgive my sin, not that You forgive it for me through the intercession of an intercessor.

The Most High said: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous.﴾ ﴿And grant me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations.﴾ ﴿And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss.﴾ ﴿And forgive my father, for he was among the misguided.﴾ ﴿And do not disgrace me on the Day they are resurrected,﴾ ﴿the Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, ﴾ ﴿except one who comes to God with a sound heart.﴾

Know that when God the Most High related Abraham's praise of God, peace be upon him, He then mentioned his supplication and his request. This is an alert that placing praise before supplication is of great importance. The verification of this matter is that these human souls are of the same kind as the angels. Whenever their occupation with the knowledge of God the Most High, His love, and their attraction to the world of spirituality is more intense, their resemblance to the angels is more complete, and so they become stronger in exercising influence over the bodies of this world. And whenever their occupation with the pleasures of this world and their immersion in the darknesses of these corporeal things is more intense, their resemblance to the beasts is greater, and so they become more incapable, weaker, and less influential in this world. Therefore, whoever wishes to occupy himself with supplication must precede it with the praise of God the Most High and the mention of His greatness and majesty, to the extent that through that remembrance he becomes absorbed in the knowledge and love of God and comes to resemble the angels closely. Through that resemblance he attains a divine, heavenly power, and so he becomes the source of the occurrence of that thing which is the object of the supplication. This is the uncovering of the reality of supplication, and it becomes clear that placing praise before supplication is obligatory. Through this, the verification of his words, peace be upon him, is manifested, relating from God the Most High: "Whoever is so occupied with remembering Me that he does not ask Me, I shall give him the best of what I give to those who ask."

If someone says: Why did Abraham, peace be upon him, not restrict himself to praise, especially since it is also narrated from him that he said: "My asking is sufficed by His knowledge of my state"? The answer: He, peace be upon him, only mentioned that while he was occupied with calling the people to the Truth. Do you not see that he said: ﴿For they are an enemy to me, except the Lord of the worlds﴾, and then he mentioned praise, and then he mentioned supplication? This is because the lawgiver necessarily must teach the Law. As for when he was alone with himself, and his purpose was not to teach the Law, he would restrict himself to his saying: "My asking is sufficed by His knowledge of my state."

The second discussion: concerning the matters he requested in the supplication, which are several requests.

The first request: his saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom (ḥukm) and join me with the righteous.﴾ God answered him when He said: ﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter he will be among the righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:130]. On this there are several points:

First: It is not permissible to interpret ḥukm (wisdom, judgment) as prophethood, because prophethood was already attained. If he requested prophethood, then the prophethood requested would either be the very prophethood already attained or something other than it. The first is impossible, because attaining what is already attained is impossible. The second is also impossible, because it is impossible for one individual to be a prophet twice. Rather, what is meant by ḥukm is the perfection of the theoretical faculty, which is through the apprehension of the Truth. And from his saying ﴿and join me with the righteous﴾ is meant the perfection of the practical faculty, which is by being one who acts with good. For the perfection of a human being is that he knows the Truth for its own sake and the good for the sake of acting upon it. He placed his saying ﴿My Lord, grant me ḥukm﴾ before his saying ﴿and join me with the righteous﴾ because the theoretical faculty takes precedence over the practical faculty in both nobility and essence. Also, it is possible for him to know the Truth without knowing the good, but the reverse is not possible. Also, because knowledge is an attribute of the soul and action is an attribute of the body, and since the soul is nobler than the body, knowledge is superior to action. We have explained the knowledge of things as ḥukm because a human being does not know the realities of things unless he brings into his mind the images of their quiddities, then attributes some of them to others by negation or affirmation. That attribution is ḥukm. Then, if the mental attributions correspond to the external attributions, the mental attributions become impossible to change, and so they become firm and strong. Such apprehension is called ḥikmah (wisdom) and ḥukm, and this is what is meant by his, peace be upon him, saying: "Show us things as they truly are." As for ṣalāḥ (righteousness), it is the rational faculty being in the middle between the two vices of excess and deficiency, because excess on one side is deficiency on the other side and vice versa. So righteousness is not attained except through moderation. Since true moderation is one thing that does not admit division at all, and human thoughts in this world are limited to apprehending such things, there is no escape for humans from departing from that limit, however slightly. But the departure of those brought near (to God) from it occurs in such a small degree that it is not perceived, while the departure of the disobedient from it is extremely gross. From this, the verification of what has been said becomes clear: "The good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near." And it becomes clear why Abraham, peace be upon him, needed to say: ﴿and join me with the righteous﴾.

The second request: Since it has been established that what is meant by ḥukm is knowledge, it is established that he, peace be upon him, asked God to give him knowledge of God the Most High and His attributes. This indicates that the knowledge of God the Most High does not come into the heart of the servant except by the creation of God the Most High. His saying ﴿and join me with the righteous﴾ indicates that the servant being righteous is only by the creation of God the Most High. To interpret these things as lutf (divine grace that facilitates obedience) is far-fetched, because according to the opponent, whatever lutf is within God's power, He has already done it. So if we directed the supplication toward it, that would be a request for attaining what is already attained, which is invalid.

* * *

The third request: The wisdom sought in the supplication is either the knowledge of God or of something other than Him, and the second is false. This is because a person, while he is occupied with the knowledge of one thing, cannot simultaneously be occupied with the knowledge of another thing. So if the object of this supplication were knowledge of other than God the Most High, and knowledge of other than God is a hindrance to being absorbed in the knowledge of God, then this request would be a request for something that would preoccupy him from being absorbed in the knowledge of God the Most High. That is impermissible, because there is no perfection beyond that absorption. Therefore, the object of this supplication is the knowledge of God. * * *

The third request: The wisdom sought in the supplication is either the knowledge of God or of something other than Him, and the second is false. That is impermissible, because there is no perfection beyond that absorption. Therefore, the object of this supplication is the knowledge of God. Then, that knowledge is either the knowledge of God the Most High that is the condition for the validity of faith, or something other than it. The second request: his saying: ﴿And grant me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations.﴾ On this there are three interpretations:

The first interpretation: He, peace be upon him, began by asking for what is the essential perfection of a human being in this world and the Hereafter, which is the request for ḥukm, that is knowledge. The internal ones: outward form and inward form. The outward form is more corporeal, and the inward form is more spiritual. So Abraham, peace be upon him, left the corporeal matter, which is the outward form, and requested the spiritual matter, which is the inward form. This is what is meant by his saying ﴿and join me with the righteous﴾. As for the external ones: they are wealth and status. Wealth is more corporeal, and status is more spiritual. So Abraham, peace be upon him, left the corporeal matter, which is wealth, and requested the spiritual matter, which is status and a good remembrance that remains throughout time. This is what is meant by his saying ﴿and grant me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: God gave him that through His saying: ﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt 37:108].

The first, in the language of wisdom: We have explained that human souls have influence in general, but some of them may be weak and thus incapable of influence. When a group of them gathers, their collective strength may achieve what individuals could not. This meaning is observed in corporeal influences. The second, in the language of perfection: Whoever becomes praised among people because of the virtues he possesses, that praise and that fame become a motive for others to acquire similar virtues.

God the Most High then granted him that, because you do not see any religion's adherents except that they revere Abraham, peace be upon him. Some objected to this, saying that the desire to praise a disbeliever is not appropriate. The answer: The intention is not to praise the disbeliever as a disbeliever, but rather that he be praised by every person and beloved in every heart.

The third request: his saying: ﴿And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss.﴾ Know that when he requested the happiness of this world, he then requested the happiness of the Hereafter, which is the Garden of Bliss. The fourth request: his saying: ﴿And forgive my father, for he was among the misguided.﴾ Know that when he finished requesting the worldly and otherworldly happinesses for himself, he requested them for the person most closely attached to him, which is his father. This view is weak, because praying on this condition is permissible for a disbeliever, so if his supplication were conditional, God would not have forbidden him from it.

The second interpretation: the sound (salīm) is the one stung (ladīgh) by the fear of Allah the Exalted.
